speechtext: Before the Orders of the Day are called, I would like to inquire from the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals and the hon. I brought this matter to the attention of the House a week ago yesterday. Neither hon. gentlemen were present, but I presume the right hon. the First Minister communicated with them. Owing to these railways not connecting at Brockville, the public is put to great inconvenience, but I do not complain of that so much as the delay in the delivery of the mails. All the mails from Toronto to Brockville gathered by the Grand Trunk Railway, arrive at Brockville a short time after the train has left for the capital. The mail bags are thrown off at Brockville a little after three o'clock in the afternoon. They remain there until the next morning and reach Ottawa between 9 and 11 o'clock in the morning, so that there is only one mail from the west. I presume that the Postmaster General has taken action in this matter in order to bring about a change in that respect. He pays the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Grand Trunk Railway for carrying mails, and I am quite certain that the people living between Toronto and Brockville are entitled to a better service than they have at present.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to call attention to a matter which is of vital interest to the fishermen of the maritime provinces, more especially to the fishermen engaged in deep sea fishing, along the Newfoundland shore. I observe in this morning's ' Citizen ' an item headed :
TREATY IS SUPERSEDED Newfoundland Fish to enter United States Free of Duty.
Valuable Monopoly Granted to an American Syndicate which will be able to get Its Products Duty Free into the United States.
This, I may say, Mr. Speaker, is simply an attempt of a renewal of the former Bond-Blaine treaty that had been brought about unfortunately in the year 1890 by Mr. Bond, now Sir Robert Bond, with the Secretary of the United States. Mr. But.no. The fishermen of the maritime provinces, realizing at that time the unfortunate position in which they would be placed by this treaty, appealed to the government then in power and met with a very favourable response. The government appealed to the imperial government through the Secretary of State, and action under the Bond-Blaine treaty as proposed, was withheld. Since then, an effort has been made during the regime of the present government to resurrect this treaty and at that I time I again brought the matter up in the I House and asked the government to intercede with the imperial authorities in order to have the matter treated in the same manner as it had been previously treated. I do not know, however, what action was taken at that time, but nothing was done. We now find by this reference in this morning's ' Citizen ' that they are again endeavouring to bring this about under the Bond-Hay treaty. This has been very strongly advocated by Sir Robert Bond, the premier of Newfoundland, and it is now before the Foreign Relations Committee of Congress with the hope of 1 its being ratified. This treaty I consider is not altogether in the interests of the fishermen of Newfoundland, as was shown when the effort to secure this treaty was previously made, for the reason that if the bait of Newfoundland is to be disposed of as proposed by this treaty, the bait fish will be used up by the Americans when they should be

preserved for the fishermen of Newfoundland, in order that they may secure the fish in their own waters. When that effort was made in 1890, we appealed very strongly to have its passage annulled, because when our fishermen visited those shores they would be compelled to purchase bait from the Newfoundland fishermen and that only in limited quantities, quite insufficient in many cases to enable them to successfully prosecute their industry. We felt that under these circumstances we would be handicapped to such an extent that the fishing fleet which is the pride of the county I represent, would be practically annihilated. I would ask the government, therefore, under the circumstances to take the matter into their very serious consideration, and take such steps as will preserve to our fishermen the opportunities which they have a right to enjoy and to see to it that the interests of the fishermen of the maritime provinces are guarded, fostered and promoted. The fishermen last year were seriously handicapped owing to the want of bait fish, which were very scarce on the shore at that time, and as a result their success in fishing during the past season has not been by any means what they would have desired. Under this treaty a company is to be formed known as the Newfoundland Cold Storage Company, with a capital of one half million dollars, but it states here that that capital may be increased to something like three millions, which would, constitute- a complete monopoly. Such a company would gather up all the fish from the various fisheries which would be placed in its cold storage plant, and as a result we might be deprived entirely of any bait for the deep sea fishermen visiting the Newfoundland coast. I therefore feel that the government will see for themselves the deprivation which the fishermen of the maritime provinces will suffer if such an arrangement as proposed is carried out. It is a matter which I feel is of vital importance to the fishermen of the maritime provinces, and I would not speak so earnestly in the matter now, if I did not feel that their interests would be completely sacrificed if this treaty is ratified.

Might I ask my hon. friend if he is not mistaken in speaking of the Bond-Hay treaty. I think they expect to get the concession under the Anglo-American treaty of 1818, because I know that the same question came up in Ontario. Americans claimed that under this treaty any American fisherman had the right to bring fish into the United States.

Under the treaty of 1818, there has been an expression of doubt as to whether American fishermen could go on that shore and fish. That question was brought up before when the treaty was referred to in 1890. Dut subsequently the matter was dropped, and I think that
is simply a reference by some American writers which has had no material effect as respects the ronritime provinces.

This despatch, which is dated from Toronto, is as follows :-
Toronto, April 26.-The ' Globe ' to-day gives prominence to a letter by Norman Smith writing from St. John's, Nfld., under date of April 19, detailing the facts of the establishing of an extensive fishing industry in that island by an American syndicate, as follows :
A Bill passed last week by the legislative assembly of Newfoundland has rendered very remote the ratification of the Bond-Hay treaty. The island has long been desirous of completing a reciprocal arrangement with the United States under which Newfoundland fish should be allowed to enter free of duty in return for fishing privileges conceded to Americans on the shores of the colony. In 1890 Mr. (now Sir) Robert Bond negotiated in Washington what is known as the Bond-Blaine treaty. Canada protested against the ratification of the treaty, and had sufficient influence with the imperial government to successfully prevent its being signed, Newfoundland resented Canada's action, and in and out of season worked hard to have the embargo removed.
Last year its representations were effective, and Premier Bond immediately opened correspondence with Secretary Hay. Soon afterwards the Bond-Hay treaty, based on the Bond-Blaine agreement, was drawn up. The treaty is now before the Foreign Relations Committee of Congress, and strong hope has been expressed in the island that, despite the strenuous opposition of American fishery interests, it would be ratified.

The Bill which the assembly of the colony has just passed provides for the granting of assistance to a United States company which proposes to go into the cold storage business on a large scale. The company is guaranteed for twenty years a dividend of 5 per cent per annum on a capital of half a million dollars on condition that $250,000 is spent on a cold storage plant and $200,000 expended yearly in the purchase of fish in the island for export. The company also undertakes to preserve bait in cold storage, and distribute the same at a reasonable price wherever it is needed by Newfoundland fishermen, an undertaking that will undoubtedly be a great boon to the fishermen, enabling them, as it will, to overcome the difficulty they have hitherto laboured under, of frequently being unable to obtain bait in localities where fishing is good.

maintopic: SHIP FISH INTO UNITED STATES FREE.

speechtext: The company, as has been said, intends to go into the business on a very large scale, and instead of being capitalized at half a million, it will probably issue stock to the extent of two or three millions, and instead of spending $250,000 on a plant, a million will be nearer the mark. It proposes to establish a central cold storage station, and a number of sub-stations

in various parts of the island. At these substations flsli will be purchased, shipped to the central depot and thence to the United States.
The American duty on fish, both fresh and dried, averages about three-quarters of a cent per pound. The Bond-Hay treaty looks to the removal of the duty on dried fish, the Washington authorities refusing absolutely to consider any change In respect to fresh fish.
The Newfoundland Cold Storage Company, the concern which has been given assistance by the [DOT] island government, will be able to ship fish, both fresh and dried, into the United States free of duty, and this is how it can be done :
The law department at Washington has given an incontrovertible opinion that, under an Anglo-American treaty signed In 1818, any American citizen may fish in certain waters of Newfoundland, and that the fish so caught in such waters are not liable to duty in the United States. On representations from the Newfoundland Cold Storage Company that certain disabilities exist preventing Americans from deriving full benefit from the treaty concessions, and that it proposes to remove those disabilities by employing Newfoundland fishermen to assist in supplying the chmpany with fish, the Washington authorities have declared that there is nothing to prevent all the fish shipped in American bottoms by the company to the United States from entering free of duty, even though not entirely caught by American fishermen.
In other words, the company referred to can apparently take into its employ if it chooses, all the Newfoundland fishermen, and ship the product of their labours into the United States free

The leverage the Newfoundland government has hitherto used in its endeavour to obtain concessions from the United States has been that at any time it could enforce a Bait Act against American fishermen, such as that now in operation against the French, or raise considerably the license fee now imposed. All the advantages of the agreement will not by any means be on the side of the company. The island fishermen will undoubtedly benefit very considerably. They will obtain not only all the advantages of the Bon*d-Hay treaty, but their fish will be admitted into the United'states free ; they will have the benefits of a great modern cold storage system, and in addition it will be enabled to obtain frozen bait in localities where bait is scarce.
So valuable is the concession to the company, however, that there is very little likelihood of the government being called upon to make up any deficiency in the profits.
The Newfoundland government still expects to put through the Bond-Hay treaty, but to everybody who has studied the details of the concession granted to the American company, no reason is apparent why the Washington government should do anything. When the Gloucester interests are informed of the proposals cf the company there probably will be wigs on the green ; but the Newfoundland Act has been duly signed, and the Washington law authorities have given an opinion in writing that would be extremely difficult to upset.
This, Mr. Speaker, you will see will handicap us to a very great extent. With the tremendous output they expect to have of bait fish it will handicap the maritime provinces fishermen employed in the deep sea fishing in going to these quarters for bait. It will not only hamper them in the obtaining of bait, but it will hamper them as well in the price, and it will mean that the industry will he wiped out completely. The ship building industry which is a very material industry, and one from which we gather, particularly in my county, a large amount of profit, will suffer a depression which will affect a large class of men, ship builders, blacksmiths, carpenters and every one else employed in connection with that industry. Under these circumstances I appeal very strongly to the right hon. premier in this connection, and I ask him to take active and early measures to meet the situation that I have pointed out. I move the adjournment of the House.
Right hon. Sir WILFRID LAURIER (Prime Minister). Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that, as has already been pointed out by the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule), my hon. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. Kaulbach) has not really apprehended the point of the information contained in this letter. My hon. friend opened his remarks by expressing the hope that the government would interfere to prevent the ratification of the Bond-Hay treaty as the government of Sir John Macdonald did in 1891 to prevent the ratification of the Bond-Blaine treaty. But. as has been stated in this letter, and which is a matter of common information, the Bond-Hay treaty has been suspended in the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations. It was referred two years ago to the Committee on Foreign Relations, it has never come out of the committee yet and it has practically been suspended. But.

as lias already been stated by the bon. member for East Grey the point is not at all whether the Bond-Hay treaty is ratified or not ratified. If the information contained in this letter is correct, it matters not at all from the point of view of the apprehension of my hon. friend whether the Bond-Hay treaty is ratified or not. The complaint made in this letter, or rather the facts brought to the attention of my hon. friend, are that the legislature of Newfoundland has organized and subsidized a company to export fish to the United States, to supply bait to American fisherman, to have American capital employed in the island to supply the bait and also to allow them to use their privileges with the expectation that these fish will be shipped to the United States free of duty. Whether, under such circumstances, fish could be exported to the United States free of duty, seems to be altogether a matter of domestic concern to the United States government, as to which we cannot have a voice, and as to which any action we might take would be absolutely without effect. My hon. friend has more reason to look with hope to the action of the Gloucester fishermen, because I see that the correspondence says, that as soon as the tenor of this new Bill passed by the Newfoundland legislature is known in Gloucester, there will be wigs on the green. I have information that already some action has been taken within the last two or three days, by the Gloucester fishermen. I have received from the United States, certain resolutions passed by the Gloucester fishermen, strongly protesting against any action which would deprive them of the rights which they have always claimed. If it were a matter in which the application of the Bond-Blaine treaty were involved, there would be some point in the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. Kaulbaeh). So far as I can see at present, the action of which'he complains has no relation whatever to the Bond-Blaine treaty, but is a matter of domestic concern for the Newfoundland legislature, and for the American Congress.

I am fully aware that we cannot interfere with any action that the United States may take in Congress in regard to their domestic relations ; but the strong point is there set out, that the Gloucester fishermen are interfering with the action of the United States, and on the same principle I to-day ask this government it they will interfere to protect the interests of the fisheries of the maritime- provinces? I think that could be accomplished through the Secretary of State of the Colonies, and by a reference to our sister colony of Newfoundland. If we are to be deprived of the. free capture of bait-fish on that shore, the United States will be in the harvest field, gathering the harvest, whilst we are deprived of getting the material wherewith to gather. I wish the Prime Minister
to see the matter in that light, and to use his utmost efforts, as I am sure he will, to place the matter in its proper position in the interests of our fishermen.

I appreciate what the Prime Minister has said so far as it relates to a purely domestic regulation of the United States, with regard to customs. It is perfectly clear that we can-net interfere with that, but at the same time this seems to be an indirect and somewhat ingenious mode of arriving at some of the results at least, which were to be accomplished by the Bond-Blaine Treaty. As far as the exportation of fish into the United States is concerned, I suppose the best we could say would he this :	that the government
should see that our own fishermen organized in the same way. should receive equal treatment in the United States, with the treatment accorded to the proposed company Blit the main difficulty, as I understand it. is. that there will be a monopoly of the Newfoundland bait possessed by this company. and in that way our own fishermen will be shut out from getting bait. I cau assure my right hon. friend, that that is a very serious condition of affairs for the fishermen of the maritime provinces, and no one can appreciate it better than some gentlemen on the other side, especially my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) who has taken a good deal of interest in this matter ; at all events, so far as our in shore fisheries are concerned. I really do not know what the future of the Ushering industry-particularly in the county of my hon. friend from Lunenburg-is to be, if this American company, obtaining these special privileges from the legislature of Newfoundland, shall possess practically a monopoly of all the bait in Newfoundland waters. Our fishermen have a great deal of difficulty there now. I have had occasion on behalf of some of my own constituents, to bring to the attention of the departments of the government, matters which are very annoying and very irritating, and as to which up to the present time, I have not been able to get any satisfaction. But, if in addition to all that, we are to be practically excluded by an arrangement of this kind, from the bait of Newfoundland, it is a matter that demands the most serious and earnest consideration of the government at the earliest possible moment. I realize the difficulties which have been mentioned by the Prime Minister, but it may be possible that these difficulties ean be overcome. It may be possible that there can be a friendly representation from this government to the government of Newfoundland, in which we shall insist that Canadian fishermen shall have at least the same right to obtain bait in the waters of Newfoundland as is accorded to American fishermen, or to this company organized by United States capitalists. I will not say any-

212S
thing further about the matter to-day, because I do not fully understand it, and of course outside of the newspaper reference, none of us have yet had time to investigate. However, it is a question that will stand investigation, and as to which we should take urgent and energetic action at the earliest possible moment.

Although the county from which I come, is not directly interested in this matter, yet the people of Nova Scotia generally are enormously interested, and especially is that the case in the county of Lunenburg, in which the iishing industry has developed to an enormous extent. If we are deprived of the right to obtain a sufficient quantity of bait, the advantages which we otherwise could secure by the nearness of our coast to the great fishing banks of the Atlantic, will be altogether nullified. Nothing too strong can be said by the representatives of the maritime provinces to impress on the government the seriousness of the situation. I was glad to note from a remark made by the Prime Minister, that he has had this matter in cognizance already, and has received some information in connection with it. I would urge him to do everything in his power, as he may very legitimately do, to make representations to the government of Newfoundland, so as to preserve the very great interests of the maritime provinces in these fisheries. The county of Lunenburg has attained an enormous development in the fishing industry, and similar development is quite possible for the counties along the Atlantic coast, and even for some of those within the Gulf of St. Lawrence, so that this is a matter not only of local, but of rational importance.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance).
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is one phase of the matter that I would like to say a word upon. My hon. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. Kaul-baeh) has referred to the desirability of our government interfering to prevent the consummation of what was once the Bond-Blaine treaty, but which now might be described more correctly as the Bond-Hay Treaty. I want to say to my hon. friend (Mr. Ivaulbach), and to others who have not given so much attention to the subject as he has :	that our friends in
Newfoundland are exceedingly jealous as to references of that kind. I have the means of knowing, and I state on the highest authority, that much of the hostility which now prevails in Newfoundland towards suggestions of union with the Dominion, is based, or alleged to be based, upon tb' attitude which we in Canada, have from time to time taken in relation to negotiations between the United States and Newfoundland. Newfoundland is a small colony, but Newfoundland is as much an independent colony as the Dominion of Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
Canada, and any assumption on our part of a right to interfere with her independent action, would naturally be resented. We would resent it ourselves, if we were hr the place of our friends in Newfoundland. Therefore, I would strongly urge that hon. gentlemen who may be giving attention to this question, should not approach it from the point of view of urging that we have any right to interfere with Newfoundland's position to as an independent colony. It is complained that we have done so in the past, it is claimed that the late government did so ; it is claimed that the present government have done so. and I know from the highest authority in Newfoundland that that line of action, so far as it had any foundation in Canada, has been the means of causing very much discontent among the people of Newfoundland towards Canada. We may do something by friendly negotiations with the statesmen of Newfoundland, an with the colonial office, but I submit that in all these negotiations, while we should be justified in doing what is best in our own interests, we must always do so subject to the recognition of the fact, that Newfoundland, although a small colony, is in every respect as independent as Canada is, and that we have no right to dictate to her. or to interfere with the manner in which she shall conduct her negotiations with the imperial government. Therefore, anything we may do, should be done in the way of friendly negotiations with Newfoundland, and not in the way of asserting any right to interfere with her action as an independent colony.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a word or two on this subject. I recognize, quite as fully as the hon. gentlemen who have preceded me, the importance of this great industry, and the most important feature in connection with it is the question of bait. I do not see how we can interfere with Newfoundland chartering a company and giving it whatever powers it sees fit ; but I think we can do something in another direction to remedy any evil which might result from its action. My suggestion would be that the government take hold of the matter of supplying bait to the fishermen. Already a good deal has been done in that direction, with good results ; but I think a great deai more could be done, and it would be worth all the time and money spent, by establishing bait depots accessible to the fishing fleet. At the present time the Newfoundland bank fleet spent at least one-half or two-thirds of their time in sailing around hunting for bait, whereas if there were a depot with refrigerators maintaining a supply for the whole season's work, these vessels could go there and be sure of obtaining a supply at all times. Then it would matter very little what action the province of Newfoundland might take in this connection. This is a

matter which has engaged my attention for some time, and I intended bringing it to the attention of the government before the close of the session. I am glad to have this opportunity of expressing these views, and I know I am not alone in holding them. The matter interests many in the maritime provinces who are engaged in that great industry. and it is a great industry, the value of which is increasing very rapidly.

Mr. Speaker, this question lias been brought to the attention of the people of this country in a very interesting and instructive manner by a special correspondent of the Toronto ' Globe ' who has been sent to Newfoundland. In yesterday's issue of that paper this whole question is discussed very instructively and very entertainingly. I regard it as a matter of so much importance that this morning I addressed a letter to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries upon it. It may be that the correspondent in question is not in possession of all the facts, or at least is not in possession of the facts as accurately as we ought to have them. This matter, as the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Kaulbaeh) has said, is of sufficient importance to warrant this government in taking every possible means to ascertain what is being done and what can be done in the way of securing to the fishermen of the maritime provinces all the rights they enjoy at the present time, and even further rights. I would therefore urge the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to take steps at as early a date as possible to inquire into this matter, and ascertain from the Newfoundland authorities what has been done and what is proposed to be done with regard to this matter.

Mr. Speaker, with your permission I would offer just a word. My hon. friend from Annapolis (Mr. Wade) has referred to the supply of bait on our own shores. A supply of bait in cold storage on our own shores would not be of advantage to Canadian fishermen visiting the Grand banks. They fish at some considerable distance to the east of St. John's Newfoundland ; and by the time they went to Nova Scotia for a supply of bait and returned to the banks where the fish may be found, the bait would be utterly worthless, unless they had a speedy or quick passage to and from. I have the most friendly feeling towards Newfoundland, and this Dominion is very warmly attached to her sister colony, who, we all feel, would not hesitate for one moment to come info the union with Canada if she realized the mutual advantages that would result from that union. This can be accomplished, however, irrespective of this question of bait which I have thought proper to bring to the notice of the government. The fact that the matter has been entered upon in a friendly spirit will, I feel sure result beneficially to the fishermen of Can- 1 68
ada. But information being obtained from the United States as to the position in which the treaty will place us as a sister colony in regard to the procuring of bait will endeavour to hamper us as far as possible.

FIELDING (Minister of Finance) Mr. Speaker, before the Orders of the Day are called I may be permitted-a motion for adjournment having been made and lost, and it not being in order to make another-to make a statement of a personal character in reply to an observation made by an hon. gentleman opposite. I can only do so by the consent of the House ; and unless I am likely to have the unanimous consent for that purpose, I shall be compelled to allow the matter to remain over until to-morrow.
Go on.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If there be no objection I will make the explanation now. I desire to invite the attention of the House, as a question of privilege, to a statement made recently in debate by the hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart). I was not in the House when he spoke, and the report of his speech did not come under my notice for several days. The hon. gentleman said :
And the Finance Minister, who has been reading a lecture to the leader of the opposition ; we all know what he did. A confidential memo, prepared for my colleagues containing an estimate, based on all the applications no matter from whom, that has been made for subsidies for different railways, and sent by me to council, was used openly in the House, and the statement was added that I had submitted to my colleagues a certain estimate for financial requirements which was greatly in excess of that brought down by the Finance Minister himself. Not only did they make use of a private memo, which was prepared for council, but they justified it and falsified it, too.
This charge, Mr. Speaker, is now made for the first time, although it seems to have reference to discussions that occurred some seven or eight years ago. I submit that if there were grounds for complaint, the charge should have been made at the time referred to, when the facts were fresh in the minds of all concerned, and when if necessary an intelligent inquiry could have taken place.



But since the charge is made even at this late day, I desire to give it the fullest and most emphatic contradiction.
At the time referred to, mention was made of certain supplementary estimates said to have been prepared by the late government in 1896, and not submitted to the House. These estimates were never claimed by hon. gentlemen opposite to be confidential papers. It was freely stated that they had been distributed among Conservative candidates and used at the elections. One Conservative private member spoke of them in the House in my hearing and mentioned a part of what they contained. Hon. Mr. Foster, who discussed the subject here, did not claim that they were council papers or confidential papers of any kind. His contention was that they were merely memoranda prepared by departmental officials and never dealt with by council.
As to the special accusation of the hon. member for Lanark that I used in this House a confidential memorandum prepared by him in relation to railway subsidies, I not only give the statement the most emphatic denial, but I am utterly unable to understand to what the hon. gentleman refers. I believe that he is labouring under a mistake.
I state in the most positive and unqualified terms that I never used in debate, in this House or elsewhere, any such confidential paper as the hon. gentleman refers to or any other confidential paper whatever.

Mr. Speaker, it is some years since there was a debate in the House in which the hon. Minister of Finance accused the late government of having brought down estimates largely in excess of what this government brought down. He stated that those estimates had been approved of by council. The fact of the matter was that they were estimates prepared in each department, notably in the Department of Railways and the Public Works Department, for presentation to council ; and every application that had been made to these departments was embodied in those estimates for the information of the colleagues of the Minister of Railways and the Minister of Public Works ; but they were never decided upon by council. We were defeated before we had an opportunity of passing upon them. Yet the hon. minister brought up, in justification of his introduction of an immense budget, the fact that the opposition, when they were in power, had introduced those estimates. I say they were a confidential document. I know that none were given out of my department to any member of parliament. I was making a comparison between the course of the Minister of Finance in using them and the course of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition in introducing and speaking on the confidential memorandum of Mr. Blair. Here was a do-Mr. FIELDING.
cument which the hon. gentleman says was prepared for council, but the estimates in which were only submitted for the consideration of my colleagues and not for presentation to the House. After reading the applications sent in, we selected those which we thought worthy of being reported to council and embodied in the estimates, to be passed upon by the council and not necessarily submitted to the House, and it was because this memorandum was represented as containing the estimates decided upon by council that I used the language my hon. friend objects to. I intended it in no sense to be personal, and have not the slightest objection to withdrawing it, if offensive.
These estimates were prepared in different departments and not to be distributed. None that I know of were ever distributed to any members of parliament. The intention was to bring them before my colleagues, and the hon. the Finance Minister, in introducing his budget, justified it by the swollen amount of these I had prepared for my colleagues.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I certainly agree with my hon. friend that our relations have always been most agreeable, and I am glad to hear that he had no intention of saying anything which would disturb those relations. There were two questions involved in his statement. The one was the general question as to these estimates, concerning which he and I have made some remarks. But beyond that, he referred to a special document, a confidential memorandum prepared by himself, dealing with the matter of railway subsidies. That is the document he specifically accused me of using in this House.
I never intended anything of the kind. I did not correct my speech, but what I referred to was the estimates prepared in my department to be submitted to council.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend said :
We all know what he did. A confidential memo, prepared for my colleagues, containing the estimates based on all the applications, no matter from whom, that had been made for subsidies for different railways and sent by me to council, was used openly in the House.
I may say to my hon. friend that I could not understand what this meant, and I caused a search to be made in 'Hansard' to find out if any previous reference was ever made to it, and I am advised it was not. At all events, I say now that I never heard of any such memorandum until the question was raised here, and I was not aware there was such a memorandum. I have no recollection of ever seeing it, or using it, or discussing it, or knowing anything about it. My hon. friend now says that his remarks had reference to the general estimates and not to that particular memorandum, so that there has been a misunderstanding.

It was in reference to the genera] estimate. I referred to the speech the hon. gentleman made some time ago, and which I brought up before in the House:
We thought we were going to meet the position of the hon. gentleman and put him in an amiable mood by bringing down estimates which he himself had prepared. I quite agree with the hon. gentleman that if we had brought down those estimates, accompanied by an announcement that we expected to expend the money and effect no saving, then, undoubtedly, the hon. gentleman might have had good cause for complaint ; but the hon. gentleman will remember that, in bringing down the estimates, I made the statement-he may call it a confession if he will-that we had not been long enough in office to make ourselves familiar with all the details of the department.
I was referring to that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The estimates to which the hon. gentleman now refers were not papers in the department, but estimates laid on the table, with which the Don. gentleman was not able to proceed.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not the matter in dispute at all. The matter we were talking about was papers which had not been brought down. The particular point I took exception to was that which the hon. gentleman says he had no intention of trying to make, namely, that the particular documents he himself had prepared, and which were confidential, were used by myself.
Not at all, I was referring to the estimates altogether.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I certainly never saw such a memorandum.

No ; I had prepared a set of estimates, and that was made use of by the hon. gentleman to show that the amount required by the government which had left office was equal to any which his government were proposing to ask for.
I asked for a certain return the other day, which the hon. the Postmaster General promised to bring down. Would he kindly let me know if we shall soon have it ?
I find that the return has been prepared by the department and forwarded in ordinary course to the Secretary of State, and should be here to-morrow.
