speakeroldname: Mr. J. R. LAVELL (Leeds and Grenville).
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the portfolio of Railways and 68J
Canals, which had been held by Mr. Blair, having become vacant by the resignation of that hon. gentleman, the country was left in doubt, save as far only as official notice was concerned, as to what has become of that portfolio. Shortly after we met here in parliament a document, which was referred to in the speech from the Throne, was placed on our desks, purporting to be an agreement signed by a gentleman who described himself as Minister of Railways and Canals But throughout this debate that gentleman who, we might reasonably have expected, would be deeply interested in the question before the House, has been conspicuous by his absence. I am glad, however, to note that he is present in the House to-day, and apparently prepared to at least listen to some of the reasons why we should not sanction this agreement which he has signed. We have not heard from him any reasons why it should be confirmed. Apart from this declaration by him at the foot of this agreement that he is Minister of Railways and Canals, and has signed it in that capacity, we know nothing of him in connection with this matter. I can quite understand that he has probably been too busy, ever since he has acquired the portfolio, to attend to so very trifling a matter as that involving an expenditure of between $100,000,000 and $200,000,000. All of his time apparently has been taken up in endeavouring to ascertain how much control of the canals he will be able to keep, and how much of what is left he can prevent falling into the hands of the Railway Commission. But as that pleasant duty ought now to be over, I trust we will have an opportunity of hearing him give us some reasons for the faith that is in him and some justification for having signed this document which has been presented to the House, and concerning which such very inadequate justification has so far been given. It would certainly require a fairly vivid imagination to assume that any reasonable justification, or even excuse, has been given us for this agreement. While, as a general rule, it is rather a disadvantage for any one to take part in a discussion after the question before the House has been debated at any length, I am glad to say that that disadvantage does not exist in this case, for two reasons. One reason is that practically no attempt has been made to deal with this subject from a broad national standpoint by those who are advocating the scheme submitted to us. From the very first, we have had no intelligent reason advanced why we should engage this country in the enormous expenditure involved. When we on this side have sought for further information, for further arguments, our requests were met in silence. When we asked for bread, we did not receive even the traditional stone, unless in the shape of a stony silence. And even on the rare occasions when members on the government side did choose to address the

House, the only answer they attempted to make to our arguments was to put up men of straw and then knock them down again. We had the second reading of a Bill involving a greater liability than any other ever introduced in this House, involving more important issues, introduced without a single argument being advanced in its support-introduced simply by a nod of the head. And when, in their innocence, the opposition considered that it ought to be discussed, we found the right hon. the First Minis ter, in his amazement that any one should dare to dispute his nod, until he found insistence was useless, insist that the matter should be carried through at once, and the opposition bend to his, will as subserviently as the majority at his back.
This, Sir, is not what the opposition is for, and I believe it will be found by hon. gentlemen opposite that the people throughout the country are coming to realize the outrageous features of this agreement, to correctly understand that a proposition is being presented to the House which involves consideration of the deepest moment to the country and to realize that the clauses in this agreement are not caricatures, but are intended as sober details in an important agreement into which the government has entered with a private corporation and which it intends to force on the country. Last session we spent many months in discussing a Bill concerning what was very improperly called a national transcontinental railway. We were told an agreement had been entered into between the government and the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Grand Trunk Railway. Amendment after amendment was proposed from this side of the House in order to modify in some measure the manifestly unwise and unfair terms of that agreement. We were told that the bargain had been completed, had been entered into, that nothing further could be done, and that we must carry this agreement as it stood ; the parties who made it were responsible parties, who would stand by it. We were told that it must be carried out exactly as signed, that the good faith of the country depended upon it. The proposition as it then stood was a somewhat peculiar one. It practically meant that the government of this country compelled the people of Canada to provide money or assume a liabiliy of about seven-eighths of the cost of the transcontinental railway, and ineidently a good deal more than one-half the responsibility for the betterments of this road, which was to be handed over to a private corporation, over which the government would not have any more control than over any other railway, this private corporation being a road which is practically controlled by a foreign country, having its interests far more largely elsewhere than in Canada, We were to receive in return a tremendous rental, amounting to an unsecured promise to pay interest for Mr. I.AVMT.L.
part of the time on part of the money. That practically was the proposition submitted by the government last year, and it has been interesting while this amending Bill has been before the House this year to note that very few of the arguments which have been presented, go to the bottom of the issue, or even go deeply into the question. Hon. gentlemen opposite have practically taken what may be called the Easter hat argument. It is said that ladies always wish to wear new hats on Easter Sunday. Two Indies appeared at church each wearing an Easter hat, and as they left church, one said to the other : How beautiful your hat is. The other lady naturally plumed herself a little but her friend continued : yels, it looks almost as nice as it did last year. That is about the substance of the argument this year, almost as nice-I do not think any member has presumed to say that it was quite as nice-as it was last year. Sir, what does this agreement mean. It is the original agreement of last year, plus some bonus additions and apologies to the Grand Trunk Pacific for not giving more. The trouble about this matter from the very beginning has been the somewhat bewildering silence that has been maintained on nearly all the important points in connection with this company, silence as to the reasons for it, silence as to the facts that might justify it. It is a matter of ancient history now that practically every argument advanced by the premier when he introduced the Railway Bill last session for building the eastern" section of this road, which is the one involving the greatest responsibility, has been dropped. They have been dropped because his reasons have been so answered that it was beyond the nerve of even the most nervy of the members on the government side to again advance his argument. Other arguments were advanced in the course of the debate, but, after all, the strong argument, practically the only argument advanced with effect in favour of this Bill on the government side, was one advanced by the premier, that his followers were going to see this through. That may be sufficient for the members on the government side, but I have faith enough in the people of this country to believe that it will be found very difficult to justify such a reason as .that before the electors. What is more, the course of events shows that the premier himself believed it was impossible to justify it before the electors. The Grand Trunk Pacific, or the Grand Trunk Railway, whichever it was that was really in default in conforming exactly to the terms of the agreement into which they themselves had entered, afforded the government an opportunity to submit the original Bill, as well as any amendments asked for and allowed, to the people of the country without causing the slightest delay in any of the operations in connection with the road. When, last session, we appealed to the government to

allow this matter to come before the people of the country before finally deciding on a question of such great moment, we were told : No, it could not wait; valuable time was being lost even in that discussion, and it was simply impossible to allow the question to stand long enough to permit it to be submitted to the electors. But before the year was out the government were well aware that the agreement, as it had been entered into last year, was not going to be carried out, and that nothing whatever could be done under that agreement until after a session of this parliament. Several months elapsed after that before this House was called. There was ample time, without causing the slightest delay, to have submitted this question to the electorate and to obtain their verdict. Where is now the argument that the road could not wait ? Who has ventured to make such a statement before the House this session ? The almost hysterical appeal of last year that time would not wait has fallen flatter than any words ever uttered in this House. Time will not wait : no, time does not wait; but the Grand Trunk Pacific had to wait, and it waited for such a length of time that there was ample opportunity to make an appeal to the people of the country, and to allow the electorate to decide on a question that so vitally affects the future of this country. This plea of not being able to wait was urged last session in connection with another matter. It was proposed to build this road through what was admittedly an uninhabited country, and the opposition urged, and urged repeatedly, that we could not obtain sufficient information to enable us to decide on the possibility of such a road, or even to decide on the terminus of such a road.
That was asked for. We were told that we would be supplied with abundant information. The old words ' mountains of information ' were used. The term has almost become classic now. Information was given us. we were told. Blue-books were published, that, we were told, contained that information. These blue-books were not published so that they could be examined by hon. members of this House until the debate was practically closed and as a consequence it is not to be wondered at that these blue-books were not extensively quoted from ; in fact, I cannot recall any case in which one of these blue-books' in particular to which I refer was ever used by hon. members on the government side of the House. But, since that debate they, as well as ourselves, have had the chance to examine that book. There is only one thought that comes to a man who looks through it and that is :	What
justification was there for putting the country to the expense of printing it ? If anything. it proves conclusively that there is by no means sufficient information available to warrant this country in undertaking the enormous expenditure involved
in the building of the eastern section of this line. There has been something since said on the question, and that by a gentleman who stands high in the estimation of the people because of his past record, a gentleman who was many times quoted by hon. members on the government side of the House in support of some of the arguments thev were advancing for the building of this road. I refer to Sir Sandford Fleming, a gentleman for whom I have the highest respect and whose opinion, as far as it is based on his own knowledge, and his knowledge on many questions is extremely wide, I Would pay a great deal of attention to. In the recess time since the House last met Sir Sandford Fleming has addressed himself to this question. He addressed the Canadian Club on the subject ' Build up Canada ' and this address, as given before the Canadian Club, has been published in magazine and pamphlet form, and I understand, distributed to the members of this House.
I am informed that it is being accepted in many quarters as an argument in favour of the building of this transcontinental rail-wav, and that it has been so used on many different occasions by hon. gentlemen opposite, more in conversation, I admit, than in the House, who, recognizing the fact that Sir Sandford Fleming's name carries great weight, have quoted his opinion to people who, they have assumed, would not read the pamphlet. With all deference to the hon. member for North Renfrew (Mr. Mackie) who, I believe, claims to have more information in regard to this northern country than any other man in this House,
I think it will be admitted that Sir Sandford Fleming has as much information and can speak with as much authority on this question as any man, and yet, if Sir Sandford Fleming's address proves anything it proves that the information we have regarding that northern country is so very limited that it is absolutely essential before the location can be made within 200 or 300 miles of any single point to make further inquiries. It proves something else. It proves that the country is very varied, w mle Sir Sandford Fleming says that that country contains a good deal of good land he does not say that he knows it of his own knowledge. I refer to this because i feel that an injustice is being done to this House by one of the members of the government. I think it will be admitted that every hon. member in this House is entitled'to wide information on a matter so important as this. I think it will be admitted that if there is any member of the government who produces information from his own knowledge of that region and that if there are many places in that northern country containing untold wealth in agricultural and minerals it is well for us to know it. I find that Sir Sandford Fleming bases practically the whole of his

argument as to the richness of portions of that northern country on some information supplied apparently, by the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher). Now, I confess that when I read this, I expected that we would have heard from the hon. Minister of Agriculture. I expected that in his leisure moments, when he was not going to Japan or elsewhere, he would travel in that northern country, because he could safely go there without running any risk of having his bachelor's state changed, as, apparently, by his own statement, there are no inhabitants in those regions. But, we have not heard from the Minister of Agriculture and I think when T read a short quotation from this pamphlet, entitled ' Build up Canada ' it will be admitted that we should have heard from him, because I take it for granted that Sir Sandford Fleming wop Id not have given this information had he not been as-' sured of its correctness. Here is what Sir Sandford Fleming says in justification of his statement that the territory in question is the natural home of pulp wood and forest wealth :
What did the well informed Minister of Agriculture state in a public address delivered at Sherbrooke a few weeks back ? He spoke of this northern region as * a country in which we know there is a great abundance of splendid agricultural land, in which we know there is an enormous amount of lumber ready for the hand of man to develop.'
I submit that if the hon. Minister of Agriculture has any such information he is not doing justice to the House in not giving it to us. I want to say further that if he does not do it he misleads a very estimable gentleman, and he takes from Sir Sandford Fleming's address and Sir Sandford Fleming's pamphlet almost the only foundation that there is for saying that there is a rich country in that northern section. Now, I trust that there is a rich country in that northern section. I trust that there may be homes for millions of people up there, but I submit, that, although this matter has been under discussion for nearly a year, although this matter has been discussed from every possible point of view, we have no right to assume that the country is as has been described, until some information is given to us and we have a right to assume that no such information is available or we would have received it. If, however, there is one thing that Sir Sandford Fleming does establish from his own knowledge it is that no transcontinental railway should be built south of Lake Winnipeg or should receive any government support if it is built south of Lake \\ innipeg. This is a matter on which Sir Sandford Fleming can speak of his own knowledge, and while not quoting further from the pamphlet, although these quotations could be enlarge# i would call at-Mr. LAVELL.
tention of the hon. members of this House to the argument of Sir Sandford Fleming given of his own knowledge from facts at his own disposal which shows conclusively that any transcontinental railway built by this government or the people of this country should go north of Lake Winnipeg. But, all this simply shows that the right hon. gentleman who introduced this Rill is continuing to ask the country to go it blind, is presenting a Bill and a contract to this House and asking the support of this House for that Bill and contract without giving any reasons which appeal to intelligent men who have the interests of the country at heart. When the changes in the contract were first spoken of, it was announced that the whole difficulty arose from the fact that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company were not prepared or did not desire to make the deposit called for by the original Act in the form laid down in the Act. When the announcement was made in the Toronto ' Globe ' and in otner papers, as read yesterday by my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke), that the terms of the Act would not be carried out and that the matter would have again to come to the attention of this House, it was distinctly stated that it would be purely for the purpose of varying the terms under which the deposit was to be made. When the House met some papers were laid on the table which purported to be, and I have no doubt are a complete collection of the proposed alterations in the eon-tract and the correspondence passing between the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway or the Grand Trunk Railway Company and the government respecting the amendments which were to come before the House this session. When these papers were laid on the table, in fact almost before the papers were laid on the table of the House, it was seen that the amendments which were suggested involved a great deal more than simply a change in the conditions of the deposit.
There is another thing to which too much attention cannot be drawn, and that is, that when the government stated it would give its reasons for calling another session of parliament, the ministers had before them not only these letters and these proposed alterations in the contract, but they must have had before them in substance the actual agreement which involved infinitely more than simply a change in the nature of the deposit. I submit that the government did not treat the House or the country honestly, in making the announcement in the terms they did. When, the resolutions were first introduced, the correspondence was referred to, but attention was not directed to the fact that the contract of last session was repudiated by the Grand Trunk Railway Company ; nor could it well be asserted in truth, because it had not been repudiated by

the Grand Trunk Railway Company. Attention was not called to the fact that the men who asked for these amendments were the very men who negotiated the contract of last year ; the very men whose faith was pledged to it, according to the statements of the ministers to parliament; and that they were the same who afterwards repudiated it. So far as we have any information before us, the contract of last year was never submitted to the Grand Truuk shareholders, until it was presented to them together with the amended contract included in this Bill on the Sth of March last, it is interesting to read over these proposed alterations in the original contract. The parliamentary document which sets them forth, opens with a letter signed by Sir Rivers-Wilson, president of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. This letter is interesting. Sir Rivers-Wilson signed the contract that was attached to the Act of last session, but his opening statement in this letter of December 15, 1903, is :
I sincerely hope that we have now reached a solution.
A solution of what ? One would have thought that a gentleman who put his signature to such an elaborate document, after discussing at length its terms and details with the government, would have thought a solution had been already reached. Two months had not elapsed from the prorogation of parliament, when this letter was written by Sir Rivers-Wilson, and the very first statement in it shows that that contract, which according to the statements made by the ministers in this House was such a final agreement that it had to be followed to the very letter, and was absolutely binding on every one connected with it-two months had not elapsed when apparently both the government and the Grand Trunk Railway Company came to the conclusion, that this contract was not in the least degree final. In this letter, Sir Rivers-Wilson refers to the deposit in a very gingerly fashion ; he drops the subject very hurriedly, and he proceeds to write a paragraph which is worth while reading. In the report of the meeting of the Grand Trunk shareholders iu London, objection has been taken to the use of the word ' partners,' and the hon. member for Essex (Mr. Cowan) repudiated very strongly any report that indicated that the people of Canada were partners with the Grand Trunk Railway Company. But, Sir, long before that report had reached this House, and long before the words reported in it were uttered, we have the very word ' partners ' used in this letter of Sir Rivers-Wilson. He writes :
It has always seemed to me that the government of Canada and the Grand Trunk Railway Company, being in point of fact partners in the enterprise-the former actuated by considerations of national policy, the latter by the necessity for securing its share in the growing prosperity of the Northwest-the burden of financial liability should he shared between the two in as equable proportions as possible, but I venture to think-and this view is strongly held by my board-that too large a portion of the burden has been imposed upon the Grand Trunk Company.
Well, Sir, it is hard to understand what the president of a railway company can mean by sharing with the people of Canada in 'equitable proportions.' The complaint we made was, that under the contract of last year, the people of Canada in the end bore all the financial responsibility, but apparently Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson came to the conclusion that the government of Canada were quite prepared to assume more financial responsibility than they did in the first place. That is practically the only thing which he desired to amend in the contract according to his letter, but apparently in an interview with Mr. Hays, who is referred to in the letter, certain other proposed alterations were demanded from the government. The first of these was : That the time for the completion of that western division should be extended ; the next: That the nature of the deposit and the use of the deposit should be changed ; the next: As to the lease of the eastern division ; the next: The payment if interest on the bonds, and then a 'reference to the Grand Trunk common stock. That covers all that was asked for, and all that having been granted bv the government, I can imagine how small Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson must have felt and how intensely disappointed he must have been when he found that having obtained so easily all he asked, he might have asked for more and got it too. Now, the first thing Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson asked for, was that the time for the completion of the western division should be extended. The government granted it at once, and apparently without discussion. Then he asked, that the deposit should be changed, and that request was also granted, although not in the exact form in which it was asked for. As to his demands in connection with the lease of the eastern division and the payment of interest on the bonds, it can be said that Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson and his friends were granted considerably more than they asked. It is true that government assistance was not granted in the form in which it was asked, but it is also true that it was granted in such form that they obtained substantially more than they asked for. In fact, a careful reading of the proposed alterations in the contract as submitted by the Grand Trunk Railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific, causes one to wonder whether they were not suggested by the government rather than by the Grand Trunk Railway Company, so completely are they granted to the Grand Trunk in the supplementary agreement. That would be bad enough if that were all. But is that all ?

there are in the supplementary contract, a number of clauses that not only grant to the Grand Trunk Railway Company) everything it asked for, but it adds some entirely new conditions, so very beneficial to the Grand Trunk Pacific and so little beneficial to the country, that it can be readily understood why the president of the Grand Trunk when asking for some alterations, should hesitate even to mention them. I wish to say a word in reference to these things which were asked for and which were granted. If one takes the supplementary contract and amends last year's contract in the light of it, and sees to it that in one document is put all that the government agrees to, and all the privileges the Grand Trunk Pacific got ; and if in doing that one reads through the speeches made by the ministers last session in defence of the original contract, one cannot help wondering with exceeding amazement what on earth these ministers would have done for argument last session, had this amended contract then been before us. I say this for the reason, that practically every substantial argument that was made against the opposition last session, was based on clauses in the original contract which have been changed in this supplementary agreement. When the First Minister introduced the Bill, he laid great stress upon the fact that the government of Canada were assuming no liability in connection with the western division. He reads the covenant that the Grand Trunk Railway Company are to guarantee 25 per cent and take a second mortgage, the government having guaranteed 75 per cent and taken a first mortgage. After having called attention to the consequence of that contract, the right hon. gentleman said this :
I need not dwell upon the importance of this covenant on the part of the company. It practically takes away from the guarantee of the government all risk. There is not a dollar to be advanced by the government. We do give our credit and nothing else. And our guarantee of seventy-five per cent of the construction of the road is to be supplemented by the credit and all the backing of the Grand Trunk Railway Company itself.
That contains the argument all through of the ministers and the members on the government side to show that the country was assuming no liability with respect to the guarantee of 75 per cent. What would they have said if this supplementary agreement had been before them ? For in substance, what is it ? It takes away from the mortgage to secure these bonds the whole remedy of foreclosure. Clause 7 of the supplementary agreement goes infinitely further. It destroys the priority of the government mortgage and puts the people of Canada and the Grand Trunk Railway Company on exactly the same basis with regard to their mortgages, neither apparently having the right to foreclose. Certainly the" government mortgage cannot be foreclosed. The Mr. LAVELL. *
only remedy it gives is the placing of the railway in the hands of a receiver and dividing whatever profits there may be between the Grand Trunk Railway Company and the government, in proportion to the respective amounts of their mortgages. It takes awTay all the government's security which was announced so strongly and pressed so earnestly by the ministers last session; and it places it beyond doubt that when this guarantee of 75 per cent is given, it is given without any ' backing ' of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. The country assumes to the fullest extent the responsibility of that guarantee, and takes equal chances with the Grand Trunk Railway Company of losing money.
But, Sir, apart from these things that were asked for some reason which has not and probably never will be explained, unless this wonderful silence of the bon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Emmerson) is broken, we find a free gift from the government to the company in the form of two most important clauses in this supplemental agreement, which are more valuable to the Grand Trunk Railway Company even than most of the clauses of agreement of last year. The first of the two clauses to which I refer is paragraph 11, which sets out distinctly that if, during the currency of the lease of the eastern division, the Grand Trunk Railway Company shall have constructed any branch lines from the eastern section, and if at the end of the period the lease the government choose to take over the eastern division, then the government will take over from the Grand Trunk Railway Company all the lines that do not pay, and they will leave to the Grand Trunk Railway Company all the lines that do pay- there is no other meaning to be taken from that-and this too without taking the precaution of providing that no branch lines should be built without the consent of this parliament. Even with such a clause in the contract, the government would be acting blindly; but the fact is that these branch lines should not be built without the consent of this parliament. The fact is as these branch lines may be built innumerably and with perfect safety by the Grand Trunk Railway Company ; for they have arranged that they may experiment as much as they please, and at the end of the term they may keep what lines they please and let the country pay for the lines which they do not think it worth while to keep.
But, Sir, there is another clause in the supplemental agreement which, in the form in which it stands, gives the opportunity of changes in this contract and if of infinitely greater advantage to the Grand Trunk Railway Company than any that has yet been proposed ; and. what is more, it gives the opportunity to the government to make these changes without consulting or obtaining the approval of this House. That clause is clause 3, which it is worth reading in full :

Pending the completion of the eastern division by the government, the company shall be [DOT]entitled to lease from the commissioners, to be appointed under the said Act, and to operate such portions of the said eastern division as may from time to time be completed, but upon [DOT]such terms as may be agreed upon between the company and the said commissioners, which terms are not to be more onerous than those of the lease of the whole division by the said [DOT]contract provided for, save in so far as may be necessary to give full effect to the paramount right of the said commissioners next hereinafter mentioned, and subject always to the paramount right of the said commissioners to *use and operate the same without any payment of tolls or other compensation for such purposes as they may deem necessary or expedient in the execution of their commission.
What does this mean ? The eastern division. as defined by the Act is a road built by the government from Winnipeg to Moncton. That whole road is to be built before the lease begins. I think. Sir. that no one in this House will attempt to argue that the Grand Trunk Railway Company wants that "whole road built. That much-maligned report of the Grand Trunk shareholders, whether we find it in the Railway ' News ' [DOT]or in the reprint of the shorthand reporter's notes, which has been referred to frequently in this debate, proves conclusively that the Grand Trunk Railway people care nothing about any part of this eastern division except that part which will enable them to dome to North Bay. I do not think that is open to debate, let alone contradiction. Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson and Mr. Hays mention the road from Quebec to Moncton, though they refer to it as a necessity that was imposed upon them; but when dealing with the road, so far as it affects their interest and their operation of it, I defy any person to show that they ever spoke about any part except that part from Winnipeg to North Bay. What is more, no matter what report we read of that meeting, we find this argument advanced by Mr. Hays as being practically the only reason why the Grand Trunk Railway Company should go into this matter. The Grand Trunk Railway Company have teen carrying large quantities *of grain from the west ; but as the roads from which they have been getting this grain, are finding Atlantic ports for themselves, their trade in that grain will decrease. These roads will no longer act as feeders for them, and so, he said it is necessary for the Grand Trunk Railway shareholders to authorize the directors to make this agreement, in order that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway may become the feeder of' the Grand Trunk. It can only become the feeder of the Grand Trunk by transferring its grain at North Bay or some other point where it can make connection with the Grand Trunk system. He takes that for granted throughout when speaking with the authority of a director to men whom he had to persuade in a business transaction.
I suppose I ought to stop here and refer to the vigorous way in which the hon. Min-inister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton) declared that the whole project was going through. There was to be no change, no variation, but one could not help thinking of the number of times minister after minister said this very same thing last session. And the Minister of the Interior is one of those who last year asserted most strongly that there was not going to be any change. Well, despite all these protestations, we have a number of changes submitted to us. and we find that these changes were decided upon and submitted to the Grand Trunk shareholders before the government condescended to make them public to the people of Canada. We have now to face the fact that assertions from ministers and members on the government side count for practically nothing, and we have to look carefully at what is possible within the limits of the contract without any regard to the interpretation which the government may put upon it. Suppose, for instance, the government should experience a sort of deathbed repentance and decide that this serious waste of money involved in building this road from Quebec to Moncton shall be postponed indefinitely. In that case, even if the road from Winnipeg to Quebec were built, the eastern section would not be completed, and if the Grand Trunk Pacific chose to use the line from Winnipeg to Quebec, the question arises what then would they have to pay for it ? Under the terms of the original agreement, their payment would be trivial enough, but under the amended agreement the government could say to the company : we will allow you to use that road, you may run your trains over it without paying a cent, and we will allow you to run it for fifty years, if you will only contribute decently to our campaign fund. We will do more, we will give you a bonus for running it and keep up the repairs on it for your benefit. I am not saying that the government will do this, but I am pointing out that they can. They are providing by this amended agreement that the Grand Trunk Pacific may use any part of that eastern section which is built, provided the terms agreed upon are not to be more onerous than those of the lease of the whole division as provided by the contract. After the exhibition we have had of the way the government screwed them down in the original contract, I do not blame the Grand Trunk Pacific people for insisting on an extra condition stipulating : you must not treat us any worse than you have. But what about the people ? I suppose the Dominion treasury is big enough to stand a haul. Evidently that is the opinion of the government, since we find no provision in either contract that the Graud Trunk Pacific should pay three per cent interest on the cost of4such part of the road as they may * use. Taking the contract literally, we must

conclude that if the road from Winnipeg to North Bay be built first and the balance not started for seven or eight years or completed for fourteen years, it is just a question whether the Grand Trunk Pacific would not have the right to use that portion from Winnipeg to North Bay seven years free of rent, and then, when the whole road is completed, for seven years more, and thus start all over again. The government might very well have insisted on the Grand Trunk Pacific paying every cent expended between Winnipeg and North Bay, as that is the only part of the road they desire to be built; and while I do not want to suggest inner motives that may lead to any further bargain, I do not think that I am suggesting anything improbable when I say that we might well imagine an arrangement being entered into, under this clause of the contract, by which the government would take further" time to consider the question of constructing the balance of the line-and there is nothing to prevent the balance of the road standing over fifty years longer-and in the meantime allow the Grand Trunk Pacific or Grand Trunk Railway to use this road from Winnipeg to North Bay, not only without paying a cent, but to have besides all the repairs paid by the government. An American writer has said that these are the days, not of great statesmen, but of great bankers and railway presidents. If he were in want of an illustration, he would find it in this contract. I do not blame the Grand Trunk Pacific for making the best bargain they could, for that is their business, but we are looking at this matter from the standpoint of the Canadian people, and I submit we have no right to leave this contract in such a shape that further expenditure of millions of dollars may be made in the interest of a private corporation without this House having any further say in the matter.
Strong arguments can be used against section 11, which binds the government to buy from the company any unprofitable road that the company may build, .but that clause had better stand fifty times over than section 3. which gives an opportunity to the commissioners to allow a private corporation to get the benefit of the expenditure of millions of the people's money without making any return.
In view of what we do know about that north country and the tremendous difficulties to be encountered in the building of a railway there, it will be many years before that road between North Bay and Quebec can be properly surveyed. But that other part from Winnipeg to North Bay is better known. Surveys have been made through a good portion of that country, this great corporation will require that piece of road, and the efforts of the government and of this company will no doubt be thrown into the building of it. Under the circumstances, the building of that road from Winnipeg to Mr. LAVELL.
North Bay will be accelerated and not retarded, but as regards the other portion, going through an unknown region, which may be a wilderness or an undiscovered paradise-the part between North Bay and Quebec-years must elapse before it will be built. During all these years, under this contract, the Grand Trunk Pacific will use only the part of the road which will be profitable to build, and the road from Quebec to Moncton will in all probability not be built. We cannot be guided by the statements of hon. gentlemen opposite in view of their declarations made last session, which they now calmly contradict.' Therefore it must be apparent to every one that this clause simply permits extensive alterations to be made to the contract and great benefits given to the company at the will of the govei'nment of the day without consulting parliament, and that can be done without any apparent consideration being given, no matter what the real consideration may be. It gives an opportunity to the government to make a gift of the people's money to a large corporation without getting any return save a return for party benefit. If there were no other reasons for throwing out this contract, clause 3 is sufficient because it opens the door to such extensive changes that in comparison little else in the contract need be considered.

Mr. Speaker, I shall ask the indulgence of the House, while I make a few remarks in reference to the Bill now before us, the importance of which we all recognize. I have listened with great interest to the speeches on both sides, during this debate. If before coming here I had any doubt with reference to the matter, I can assure you that after listening to this debate, I have come to the conclusion that the Grand Trunk Pacific scheme is an unreasonable and unfair proposition to present to the people cf Canada. If I could use the eloquent words of the right hon. the premier in introducing this measure, I should say that the flood of which he spoke was a calamitous flood, I believe that this is an unjustifiable expenditure of public money and when we come to look into the maps for information before us, we begin to realize that we have no surveys or information whatever that will enable us to come to a fair opinion in reference to this measure. I cannot conceive of a body of business men coming, to this House as the government have done and proposing to expend from $150,000,000 to $170,000,000 of the people's money, without proper maps, surveys or information. Who ever heard of the pTomoters of any railway company asking peojrle to take stock in a company with so little knowledge of the road over which-the line is to travel or the obstacles to be met. The only available knowledge is furnished by a man win visited a small portion of that country

over 200 years ago. It is unfair and unreasonable to ask the members of this House to support this measure on so little information. We are told there are mountains of information in this book called ' The National Transcontinental Railway,' -the resources of this country. I would rather say in looking into that book, that there were mountains of condemnation. Is there a man in this House who would take stock in this enterprise if it was floated. I do not believe any business man on either side would venture to take stock in it, yet we are asking the people of this country to spend from $150,000,000 to $170,000,000 of their money in promoting a scheme which is not in the best interests of the Dominion, yet practically every man. woman and child in this country is to be taxed to the extent of $25 a head, to promote this enterprise. We must realize the seriousness of the step we are about to take. It looks to me too much like a game of chance. I do not believe we are sent here to take any chances with reference to the expenditure of the money of this country. Why do not the government ask a mandate from the people ? The business way would have been for the government before entering upon this enterprise to employ a staff of engineers to make reports, promptly and expeditiously. This would have aided us in giving an honest, straightforward opinion in reference to this scheme. Can you wonder at members on this side of the House wanting to investigate this side of the matter before entering into a scheme involving such an enormous expenditure ? The Conservative party are not opposed to the building of railroads, or rather they are not opposed to assisting transportation. The Conservative party have been the party of construction in days gone by. They brought about confederation, they built the Canadian Pacific Railway, and I am surprised to hear hon. gentlemen condemn the construction of that railway which was so successfully carried out by the Conservative party. The Conservative party, to a great extent, built our canals and improved our waterways. The object of the Conservative party is not to tear down, but rather to build up and construct. The Conservative party in this matter desire to extend the Intercolonial Railway on to the Pacific Ocean. The Intercolonial Railway, as you are aware, is a government road ; it has cost this country over $70,000,000, and instead of paralleling that road, we desire to extend it through to Winnipeg and on to the Pacific Ocean. Then we would have in every sense of the word, a government road, a people's read, a road controlled entirely by the government and the people of this country. By doing that we would be binding the provinces of this great Dominion together with a bond of steel. It would not only cement the provinces as nothing else would, but it would give prompt and efficient aid
to the Northwest long before it can be expected that the Grand Trunk Pacific can possibly give that aid. It would be a government road in every respect, all the rolling stock and equipment, every rail and tie, every foot of ground, from ocean to ocean, would be under the control of the government of this country. The Canadian Pacific Railway, of which we, have heard so much from the opposite side' with reference to rates, would be practically under government control. If we had the control of this road, as we naturally would have if we owned it, we would be able to ccntrol any road running from east to west across our country. That would be a guarantee that the shippers of grain from the west to our eastern ports and the shippers of goods from the cities and towns along that line of railroad in the east, would be protected from exorbitant freight rates. They will be able to ship these goods at the actual cost rate of freight.
Now, why can not we have a government road ? Is it not an opportune time ? Are the people not prepared to pay for this road ? When we come to realize that the government of this country are prepared to spend from $150,000,000 to $175,000,000 and turn that amount of money over to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, and when the Grand Trunk Railway Company say distinctly that they only expect to spend $15,000,000 more, is it not natural to expect that the people will condemn any government for not having sufficient business ability to pay that extra $15,000,000 so as to own and control the road for all time to come ? The Grand Trunk say that it would cost them $15,000,000. If the project is such a good One as hon. gentlemen on the government benches would lead us to believe, why do they not pay this extra $15,000,000 and have full control of the road? The government have no proof that the project they propose is a good one and the opposition have shown them an altogether better proposition. As was stated before in reference to the Intercolonial Railway we have spent over $70,000,000 on that road. We ignore that road and send it begging. Why not extend it and make it a paying proposition ? There is no doubt about it, Mr. Speaker, that if the road were extended as has been proposed it would be a decidedly paying proposition. That its extension will meet with the general approval of the people of this country I have not the slightest doubt. It is surely not good judgment on the part of the government to build a railway paralleling to a great extent the Intercolonial Railway. The only part of the proposed new road that is not likely to parallel the Intercolonial Railway will be located near the American border which seems to be approached with such'great fear by hon. gentlemen opposite. The Intercolonial Railway, extend-

ed as proposed, would take the freight and distribute it throughout the Northwest. Not c pound of freight could possibly go to an American port. To-day the Grand Trunk Railway Company are compelled by the shareholders of that company to have a large amount of freight shipped by way of Portland. We cannot expect that they will [DOT]carry the freight, as proposed, down to St. John and Halifax when they can have it delivered at Portland and be able to pay larger dividends to the people who own the stock and in this way increase their income. The government proposition in short, is to expend from $150,000,000 to $170,000,000 of the people's money in building a road, when $15,000,000 more would have enabled the government to have completed and owned the road from ocean to ocean. They then without maps, surveys, *or any other information, save that a rose bloomed in the spring up north, strike an imaginary line from Moncton to Winnipeg and on to Port Simpson, and they say no matter what mountains or obstacles are in the way. no matter if we can never obtain a pound of freight, they are prepared to carry it out. It does not matter whether people obtain a livelihood in those regions to the north, it is there that the railroad must run. It is the determination of the government that the railway must be built, and when we find hon. gentlemen opposite stating that they stand or fall by the proposition, we realize that they are determined to make this expenditure whether it meets with the approval of the people or not. In accepting this proposition the Grand Trunk Railway Company are running no risks. The short haul to Portland has been mentioned; the result of this arrangement is that United States ports will be built up at the expense of Canadian ports. Do you wonder at the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals saying that it was a grave and egregious error, a calamitous blunder and one which will deal disaster to the future of our country ? The government have no definite idea of where they are going to run this road nor what it will cost this country. Can you wonder then that the opposition are lighting this scheme for everything that is in them ? Gan you wonder that the people and the press of our country are demanding that the government shall accept the proposition which has been made in reference to the governmental road ? The original proposition made by the government was bad enough, but when we come to examine the arrangement which has been laid before us we realize that every word that is in the amendments, is practically a word in favour of granting something towards the Grand Trunk Railway Company, and that there is not ont word in the interest of Mr. ARMSTRONG.
granting anything on behalf of the people of our country. There haa not been a great amount of money spent upon this scheme by the Grand Trunk Railway Company as yet. Would it not be wise for the government to take into their serious consideration the proposed extension of the Intercolonial Railway. It is not for the government to say that they will not accept the scheme of the opposition when they know, as many hon. members on the other side fully realize, that as far as the opposition scheme is concerned, it is the most beneficial to the country. The government have an opportunity to unite the provinces such as they never had before. The government have an opportunity to control rates from ocean to ocean. The government have an oportunity to immortalize their names on the page of history as men, who, in a great crisis, were not afraid to change their course for the benefit of the whole country. The nation will respect the government fou having done so. Foreign lands will say:	' Progressive Canada, Canada that controls a railway from ocean to ocean, Canada that owns a railway from ocean to ocean.' They will say that Canadian statesmen are abreast of the times, that they have confidence in the future resources of their country and the names of hon. gentlemen will be heralded throughout this country and throughout foreign lands as those of men who had the best interests of their country at heart. But, what will the nations of the world think of statesmen of this or any other country who, having within their grasp the opportunity of building a railway from ocean to ocean by the spending of from $13,000,000 to $15,000,000 of money, will not accept that proposition and undertake the construction of that road for the benefit of the people ? I am afraid, Sir, that the nations will be justified in calling these statesmen followers of the man who sold his heritage for a mess of pottage. I therefore beg of hon. gentlemen opposite as men having the responsibility for six millions of people in their hands, and having hundreds of millions of industrial and commercial wealth at their disposal, that they will not throw away the greatest opportunity this nation has ever bad, that of building a railway from ocean to ocean under the full control of the government and the people of our country. If the government accept the proposal of hon. members on this side of the House the annals of the future will ring with the praises of the men, who, when a great scheme of national importance presented itself, soared above party feeling and party prejudice and accepted a plan because of its lasting benefit to our race.

Mr. Speaker, I am not vain enough to imagine, after all the speeches that have been made on this question this session, and all that was said upon it in the previous session, when it was first presented to the House, that I can say anything very new. Neither do I intend to occupy a great deal of time in discussing it. In the course of a debate such as this there will develop certain characteristics, certain features, that are particularly noticeable. One of these features on this occasion is the attitude of silence adopted by the government. The government have, I presume, a perfect right to hedge themselves about, in this somewhat difficult matter, so far as they can, in their effort to retain themselves in office, which is after all a very large element in their consideration of it. A man is not hound to criminate himself ; and if for hon. gentlemen opposite to open their mouths and declare themselves is to get themselves into greater difficulty than they were in before, it is perhaps wise on their part to adopt the policy of silence. Whatever objections I may have felt previously to this policy, when I was home the other day, I felt rather grateful to the government for not speaking. A number of people, both among my own constituents and among those whom I met on the train, said to me that they believed they had got more accurate information during the course of this debate from our side of the House in one day than they had got during the whole of last session from the members of the government. So that there is some compensation in this state of affairs, after all.	.
I do not perhaps need to say that I am opposed to the amended scheme. I endeavoured as far as I could to express my disapprobation of it as it was propounded in 1903 ; but bad as that scheme was, so far as the interests of the country are concerned, the present scheme is infinitely worse ; so that it is not perhaps necessary for any one to rise for the mere purpose of declaring his hostility to this scheme, if he was opposed to it when it was first introduced into this House. A year ago certain statements were taken from a pamphlet entitled ' Facts ' which had been issued by the Grand Trunk Railway Company, at a time when this question had not assumed the position it occupied in 1903 or the position it occupies to-day ; and taking that as a fair basis, 1 made a calculation of the cost of the project, and arrived at a result somewhat higher even than the estimates made during last session. I have had time to reflect since then, and, having regard to the additional burdens which are placed on the people by the present amendments, I venture to predict that when all is said and done, it will not cost less than $200,000,000 to carry this scheme through.
But I do not think you can quite swamp Canada by a matter of $200,000,000. I do not think that you would ruin this country altogether, even though you cast upon it a burden of $200,000,000, but X do feel that you are going to retard the prosperity of the country to a large extent. Worse than that, we are-putting ourselves under the control of the Grand Trunk Pacific and Grand Trunk Railway, and are exacting no safeguards. We are enabling them to carry our trade, if they choose, to foreign ports, which is much more serious than even the expenditure involved in this scheme. We are entering upon a contract ill manner similar, but in consequences infinitely worse than the scheme to which the government committed us in the matter of the Mackenzie & Mann railway in the Yukon. The same result is bound to happen. The government was asked to submit this matter to the people. It was urged to take this course last session, and gave us as an excuse that time would not allow of an appeal, that the contract would brook no delay. And although they could not pretend that they had a mandate from the people, still they refused to ask for a popular verdict on the question, on the excuse that delay would be fatal. Yet to-day we are in this position, that the government have done nothing since last session. They have not taken any steps to hasten the construction of this line, and there can be no doubt that the submitting of the question to the people would not retard the work to any extent, should the people declare themselves in its favour. The people are entitled to have this matter discussed upon the hustings, and considered and voted upon by them before they are involved in so huge an undertaking ; and if. after the policy has been fully discussed, they should sustain the government, I for one would willingly withdraw

all opposition to it. But as the matter now stands, should the government be defeated as I apprehend it will at the next elections, we will be in the same position as we were with reference to the Mackenzie & Mann deal. Should the government be defeated, we will have to pay, owing to the obstinacy and folly of the present administration, a large amount in order to buy back for the people the control of their own carrying trade.
Let me say that the one thing which impressed itself upon the people last year was the fact that the Minister of Railways, who. above all others, should have been consulted, was not consulted, but absolutely shut out from the consideration of the government scheme. That was very significant, and we find the same line being pursued on this occasion with regard to the present incumbent of that department (Mr. Emmerson). But what is much more serious than shutting out the Minister of Railways perhaps was the shutting out of the people of Canada from the consideration of the measure, by the government not introducing its cast iron agreement to this House until it was formally completed and signed. We had this measure introduced to this House on the 30th of July, 1903, and we find that on the 29th of July of the same year the government and the other parties to the contract signed the agreement. That resulted in this attitude being taken by the government, that when the representatives of the people wanted to discuss the matter they were told that no amendment whatever could be considered, because the contract had been completed and could not be changed. What would have been the honest course for the government to adopt during last session ? The honest and frank course would have been to inform the Grand Trunk Pacific or the Grand Trunk Railway that the terms upon which they were willing to build the road must first be submitted to parliament before the government could agree to them. Then we would have had a free discussion of the whole matter, the railway company would have been aware of the tone of the discussion, the negotiations would have been continued during the session, and by the time the House was ready to vote upon the measure, we would have had an agreement consented to by both sides. We would have had upon the one side what the company were willing to accept, and on the other what the government were willing to give, and consequently could have had a completed agreement, and thus dispensed with the necessity for calling this extra session for the sole benefit of the Grand Trunk Railway people. That course was not adopted. But another opportunity offered itself which the government could have taken advantage of to put themselves right before the people, and that was when the Grand Trunk Pacific declared that they were not prepared to carry out the terms of the agreement they previously entered into.

That was the time for the government to have put itself right, and have got from the company some fair concessions in return for those they were asking. Again, the government should not have committed itself to the supplemental agreement before getting the opinion of this House ; and I venture to say that when we are discussing this contract in committee, we will be met with just the same difficulty as confronted us a yea* ago. We will be told, here is an agreement signed by the company, these are the terms we have secured from the Grand Trunk Railway, and these terms cannot be modified in any manner. What I submit is that the government had then another chance of obtaining an absolute guarantee as to rates, and let it go. They had a chance to bind, not only the Grand Trunk Pacific, but the Grand Trunk Railway, but failed to take advantage of their opportunity. They could have obtained an absolute undertaking from the Grand Trunk Railway not merely to acquire but to purchase and pay for [DOT]$25,000,000 of stock and hold it according to the terms of the original bargain ; and, what is more important than anything else, they could have obtained an absolute guarantee that this road would be in fact, as well as in theory, an all-Canadian road, a national highway, and that the hostile interests of the Grand Trunk would not be allowed to prevail, and prevent the carrying of the products of the west to Canadian ports. Time and again have the government been asked to point to one concession to the people of Canada which has been obtained as the price of giving the additional advantages given by the supplemental contract to the Grand Trunk Railway. Not one can there be found. Who is responsible for this ? The present Minister of Railways (Mr. Emmerson) does not seem inclined to shoulder the responsibility. He either will not toe the mark, or they will not let him.
I am inclined to think that hon. gentleman would face the music to-day if the government would allow him to do so, and that as they endeavoured to muzzle the exMinister of Railways (Mr. Blair) they are to-day preventing the Minister of Railways (Mr. Emmerson) from opening his mouth upon this question. Could there be a more humiliating position for a Minister of Railways or any other cabinet minister than to be prevented from dealing with a question which especially and peculiarly pertains to his department. Some one said to-day that he was labelled ' Minister of Railways ' in order that he might sign the contract and that seems to be about the position. The present Minister of Railways has the sympathy to some extent of members on this side of the House, and although the right hon. gentleman who leads the House has not treated us on this side with the consideration we might expect from him, and which we have received from him on some

former occasions, I think that he too is entitled to our sympathy. How far the | events of last night indicate that there was a difficulty in the camp and that there was danger of the rank and file deserting the right hon. gentleman I do not know. But we have this fact that a year ago the right hon. gentleman was able to introduce this .measure in a speech which although it was lacking in cogent reasons, at all events had a happy ring about it as if the hon. gentleman had, to a large extent the support of his following in the House, and the manner in which they applauded his utterances must have been some satisfaction to him on that occasion. But contrast his manner then with the manner in which he spoke in this debate and contrast that applause with his almost total desertion by his cabinet now. In extending that sympathy we of course cannot altogether forget how that right hon. gentleman treated his colleague the exMinister of Railways (Mr. Blair) only a year ago, nor can we forget the attitude of the right hon. gentleman when at the council board, knowing that the ex-Minister of Railways (Mr. Blair) was opposed to this scheme, and yet concurred in asking that gentleman to attempt to carry it through the House or at least, if he would not give it his open countenance, at all events not to condemn it. I venture to say that it will be a long time before any other Minister of the Crown will occupy such a humiliating position as that occupied by the right hon. the premier in this regard. 1 am aware that the ex-Minister of Railways (Mr. Blair) on a subsequent occasioq pointed out that it was not the right hon. gentleman himself who urged what I cannot characterize as other than an infamous proposition, but it remains that when that infamous proposal was made, the right hon. gentleman was there and did not condemn it. and as leader of the government he stands committed to it as thoroughly and as deeply as any member of the cabinet. And, Sir, although all of the colleagues of the right * hon. gentleman were present in the House when that matter was first made public, not one of them rose in his seat and said it was he and not the right hon. gentleman who leads the House who had made the proposal. They were content to allow him to be condemned. Therefore am I not right in saying that there must be a feeling of sympathy for the right hon. gentleman by reason of what has been shown by Mr. Blair and of the desertion of the right hon. gentleman by his colleagues ? We have nice distinctions in this House. I recall the declamation, the indignation and the horror of the right hon. gentleman and the Minister of Finance the other day, at the action of the hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden). They were so solicitous of the honour of parliament which had as they alleged been tarnished by the
act of the hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden). It reminds me of the story told of a French nobleman who, by eaves-dropping discovered where a large treasure was hidden. He had no scruples about possessing himself of the treasure, and in the dark hours of night he went to the place where it was buried in the earth. When he arrived there he remembered that he had neither pick nor shovel with which to exhume the treasure, and it caused him the most abject sorrow and misery to think that he, a gentleman of such high estate, should have to descend to the meanness of stealing a pick and shovel ; but he had no qualms of conscience as to stealing the treasure hidden in the earth. The hon. gentleman's anxiety is something of that class. He has -in the political sense-robbed the people of this country of millions, he has pledged the credit of this country and got no proper value in return; he has formed a partnership with the Grand Trunk Railway Company and stands as a partner with that company to-day, although that partnership is not in the interests of Canada but is in the interests of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. This does not affect the rignt hon. gentleman's sense of honour in the slightest degree, but if we on this side, fighting for the rights of the people, get possession of a document that throws a vast amount of light on this question, that shows the true inwardness of the transaction, if we use that in the interests of the people of this country, he is shocked. I for one would have no hesitation in using such a document. Many copies of it had been printed and distributed to members of the government and I would have no hesitation in using it to safe-guard the interests of the people.
There was great urgenry in 1903, according to the right hon. gentleman. There were two grounds for this urgency. One of these was congestion in the west. It was pointed out again and again last year that the only difficulty there arose from the want of rolling stock on the Canadian Pacific Railway, and that if that road was as well equipped as the Grand Trunk and Intercolonial there would be no congestion in the west. But) there is not such urgency now. and an extension of time, of three years, has been granted in the case of the western division. The eastern division is evidently not going to be completed at any rapid rate, or we would not find the provision in the amended contract giving the commissioners the right to lease a portion of the road before the rest is completed.
Let me say just at this point that, not only is that an indication that probably the government are beginning to realize the peculiar difficulties which confront them in the matter of constructing the eastern section, and do not, perhaps, contemplate the construction of the eastern section at
