any time, east of North Bay, but it also affords an indication of just what the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company actually intend to do. What is evidently contemplated at the present time is that the necessary part of what is called the eastern section, the portion between North Bay and Winnipeg, is the only portion that the government contemplates completing and the only portion that the railway company are willing to operate, and that when that is completed, the government will lease that portion to the railway company and that is the last we will hear of a transcontinental railway for many years to come But, the great mater of urgency, that the right hon. gentleman referred to with so much earnestness and in regard to which be concluded with a prayer last year, was the fear of the abrogation of the bonding j rivilege. He was afraid it was already too late. He made that the turning point upon which he based his argument. That, above all other reasons was the reason upon which he himself had decided immediately to put into execution this great transcontinental scheme. * Heaven grant ' he said ' that already it may not be too late.' He pointed out in very graceful sentences, in very eloquent terms, that it was not a question of tomorrow, or to-morrow, or to-morrow, that it was an immediate questiou, a question of this day, of this hour and of this moment. Well, what happened? We have the fact that when the right hon. gentleman produced his amended measure, every clause of which he prefaced by an ample apology, he said not one word about the bonding privilege, because he knew the question of the bonding privilege was repudiated not only by the good sense of his own followers, but by the country at large the moment he gave expression to his fears at the last session of parliament. He dare not upon this occasion rest his case in the remotest degree upon the question of the bonding privilege. The right hon. gentleman must have known then, as every man in public life in Canada must know, that the retention of the bonding privilege is as important to the people of ihe United States as it is to the people of Canada. Go into the library and bring here the books that were read to my right hon. friend last session and you will find the statements of the most distinguished and influential men in the United States, backing up those who formed a committee to inquire into these trade relations, one and all agreeing, making no secret about it, but publishing it to the world at large, that the people of the United States are just as dependent upon Canada as Canada is dependent on the United States for the maintenance of the bonding privilege. I want to say just here and now, that, whether in the matter of the bonding privilege or in regard to any other matters, Canada must take her stand. In the matter of trade relations, the country has shown Mr. LENNOX.
that it is when Canada holds her own, and determines to take a manly attitude in regard to the United States, the people of the United States begin to respect us, to come and ask us for fair terms and to offer us fair terms in return. Take the question of reciprocity, as it presents itself to-day, and contrast that with a few years ago, and it will be admitted that there is abundant vindication of what I say. We have only to stand by our rights to teach the people of the United States that whilst we wish to have friendly relations in all matters with them, yet, we are a self-respecting people, a people quite capable of maintaining our rights, aye, and a people who are determined to maintain our rights us against all comers. Now, I said some moments ago that the right hon. gentleman in introducing his measure containing these amendments, introduced it with a good deal of apology, and in that I think he has only done what he ought to do. A year ago the right hon. gentleman assured this House, I think, perhaps, without due consideration, that this scheme was vastly beneficial to the interests of the people of this country, and that it would cost just thirteen millions of money, not twelve and a half millions nor thirteen and a quarter millions, but exactly thirteen millions of dollars. The right hon. gentleman had got it down to a fraction. The hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) followed him shortly afterwards. He had secured the services of an actuary, he had gone closely into the calculation and he had got it down to a much finer point. He did not round it out in the fine bold millions of the right hon. leader of the government, but he got it down to fractions, just so many millions, so many thousands, so many dollars and so many cents. But, his estimate was some $6,000,000 higher than that of the right hon. leader of the government. To-day we have the right hon. leader of the government telling us that certain minor concessions are asked for by the Grand Trunk Railway Company. Let me say just here that I do not understand exactly upon what basis the Grand Trunk Railway Company ask for anything. The Grand Trunk Railway Company have entered into no contract with Canada. They make no promises. They will submit to no obligation. They are no part of the company with which we are dealing. We have to rely- let the hon. gentlemen take back their words of last session as they will-upon the covenant of the contract of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company and of that company alone.
How comes the Grand Trunk Railway Company to ask for terms at all ; whence comes their right to hold a meeting iff London, England, to dictate the policy which Canada shall follow; whence comes the right of the Grand Trunk directors to say to their shareholders, that they have driven the government of Canada into a partner-

ship with them ? Taking it all in all, it is a. most extraordinary proceeding. Aside from technicalities, any person who views this as a common sense business transaction, must come to the conclusion that there cannot be a more unfortunate thing than that it is the Grand Trunk Railway which is ostensibly dealing with the government, while it is the Grand Trunk Pacific with whom we are actually dealing, and from which we are getting security-if we are getting any security at all. I believe that the consensus of opinion in Canada is, that if the government had looked over all this Dominion for a company with which to contract, they could not have found a company whose interests were more antagonistic and diametrically opposed to the interests of the people of Canada, than this same Grand Trunk Railway. I have not a word to say against the Grand Trunk Railway Company ; I am free to render them praise for anything they have done in the way of developing this country ; but I am also here to say that Canada has given the Grand Trunk Railway a full and complete equivalent in the past for anything they may have done. I say that no more dangerous thing could have been done than for the government of Canada to enter into a contract with a company which has its termini in the United States ; a company having its interests centred in the United States ; a company which has built up at vast expense terminals on the one side at Chicago and on the other side at Portland, and a company which must necessarily for its own welfare, endeavour to divert trade from Canadian to United States channels. This government may today think that they can force this measure through and ignore our warnings, but I venture to say deliberately, that it will not be very many years before the people of this Dominion will have realized that we are giving the Grand Trunk Railway a most dangerous control over the destinies of Canada, and that that control will have to be brought back at a huge price paid by our people. There was a time when we used to jocularly refer to the late Minister of Public Works (Mr. Tarte) as the master of the administration, but a change has come, and a perusal to-day of the speeches of Mr. Hays and Sir Rivers-Wilson, forces the people of Canada to the conclusion, that we have now new masters of the administration, and that in fact the Grand Trunk Railway Company is dictating the policy of this country in the matter of the Transcontinental Railway. There have been vast concessions made to the Grand Trunk Railway. A study of the correspondence between the company and the government leads to the belief that the only reason why the government have not given more to the Grand Trunk Railway is because the Grand Trunk Railway did 09
not ask for more. There is nothing for Canada, but everything for the Grand Trunk Railway Company. The right hon. gentleman may think that it is all right at present to give this enormously rich contract to the Grand Trunk Railway, but the people of this country realize, that it is an extravagant and wasteful dissipation of their resources, and that there are men in the cabinet who if they dared speak, would condemn the scheme as strenuously as I do. That being so, the right hon. gentleman will not be so jaunty over this scheme when he comes before the electorate of Canada. When the right hon. gentleman introduced the Bill a year ago, he introduced it with a great flourish of trumpets and in a speech of words, and only words, but I can tell him that the verdict of the people of Canada is, that this measure was conceived and designed largely for the purpose of placing the right hon. gentleman, if that could be possible, side by side wfith the greatest man that ever occupied a position in Canadian public life:	the right

Macdonald. The people of Canada believe that this scheme was devised, more for the purpose of aggrandizing the importance of the Prime Minister himself, than for the purpose of advancing the true interests of ''this country.
But, Sir, this railway company not content with obtaining such signal advantages from the Dominion government sought others from the government of Ontario. Have we two great Liberal parties in this country ; the one which condemns grants of lands to subsidize railways ; the other which gives away -wholesale the lands of that people to these corporations. The Ontario government have forgotten the pledges that have been made by this government in that regard and in addition to granting this company $400,000 cash for a branch line from Port Arthur to connect with the Transcontinental Railway east of Winnipeg, they have also given away 6,400 acres per mile for 200 miles, or in all 1,280,000 acres of the heritage of the people of the province to this company ; and all to divert our Canadian trade to American ports.
Where are the boasted professions of the great Liberal party of Canada, when we find these gentlemen in Ottawa making one profession and their friends and supporters in Ontario making another ? Mr. Speaker, it is very much of a piece with the way in which these gentlemen all through are assisting one another. Whenever one party is handicapped, relief comes from the other. For instance, take the case of Mr. Jackson. He became so notorious that, although I would not like to use the offensive language used by the right hon. gentleman the other night in reference to the Conservative party, and say that Mr. Jackson stunk in the nostrils of anybody, yet I say he has been guilty of such corrupt and nefarious practices that

the judges of the courts have spoken of him in a way that could not be harsher or more extreme if applied to any criminal in the land. The Ontario government, finding themselves tottering on the brink of ruin, try to maintain themselves in office by fraudulent devices. They dared not brave public opinion and appoint this criminal Jackson to a public position ; but they counted on their friends in this House, who were so shocked over the reading of the memorandum of the late Minister of Railways and Canals, and they compromised with these hon. gentlemen and got them to appoint Mr. Jackson to a good position of emolument under the Crown and send him to Great Britain. A sweet and beautiful example Mr. Jackson is, a nice object lesson of what the people of this country are to the people of Great Britain-Mr. Jackson, the criminal, sending immigrants to this country and paid by the present administration.
Speaking of this memorandum of Mr. Blair, it is not much wonder that the government got pretty indignant at the fact that it had been delivered to the leader of the opposition. The right hon. gentleman who leads the government made the statement time and again-out of the whole cloth, I think, because he jrtis not able to back it up, and it turns out to be not in accordance with the fact-that Mr. Blair was as hostile to the scheme propounded by the hon. leader of the opposition as he was to the scheme propounded by the government. What does Mr. Blair's memorandum say 7 It was opened and delivered to the members of the cabinet on the 10th or 12th of December, 1902. It advocates in the most distinct words the limited adoption of government ownership of railways, that is, the extension of the Intercolonial Railway to the Georgian Bay and ultimately to the Pacific coast. What distinction is there between that scheme and the scheme propounded by the hon. leader of the opposition 7 When the right hon. gentleman is driven from pillar to post, not knowing how to defend himself, what does he do ? Why, he finds an item in the Halifax ' Chronicle ' or some other newspaper in the maritime provinces, quoting a statement of Mr. Blair ; and what does Mr. Blair say ? He says this, and no more, that he is opposed to the immediate construction of the railway. To that extent he is not quite in harmony with the hon. leader of the opposition. Now, we are not prepared to take a second place to Mr. Blair or any Reformer in this country in regard to the development of the country. The Conservatives of Canada have always been the pioneers in the development of this great country. They have always had hopes for the country, and believed in its magnificent possibilities. It was the Conservative party that first started this country on the march of prosperity, and I believe they will soon again be in control of the helm of Mr. RENNOX.
state, bringing to it a still greater degree of prosperity.
I want to point out one significant sentence in this memorandum of Mr. Blair which should have been a warning to this government ; that is, the sentence in 'which Mr. Blair expressly and emphatically urges the government-having a premonition evidently of what they were about to do-not to enter into a contract with any railway company whose interests are at variance with -those of the people of Canada. That is exactly what the government have done. That is exactly what they have done, therefore, in face of the warning of Mr. Blair; and when this whole matter is known more fully than it is to-day, I think there will be such sidelights thrown upon the dismissal of Mr. Blair, upon the hostility of the cabinet to him, upon the treatment which he was accorded to the government as have not yet manifested themselves.
One word more, and that is in reference to government ownership. Probably the people of Canada have not come to the conclusion that all railways in Canada should be owned and controlled by the government. But I do believe that there is a universal feeling to-day that one great trunk line, sufficient to control rates, to afford adequate competition with the Canadian Pacific Railway or any other competing line, should be owned and controlled by the government. Whether that is a sound principle in itself or not, nobody who approaches this matter without prejudice, as it presents itself today in the light of the amendments that have been made to the contract, in the light of the statements which have been made by Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson and Mr. Hays at the meeting of their shareholders, and in the light of the fact that the utmost dollar which the Grand Trunk Pacific or the Grand Trunk are putting into this scheme is $14,500,000, while we are putting in probably $160,000,000-no one who considers this matter, however he may feel on the general question of the government ownership of railways, can avoid feeling that it is an unwise move on the part of the government to commit Canada to this scheme in which they will have no control over rates or over the routing of freights. When these two points are admitted, and when we are putting into the scheme such a large amount of money, why not go a little further and pay $14,500,000 or $15,000,000 more, and have this road controlled and used by the people of Canada as a great and truly transcontinental line ? I do not propose to follow this matter further. The government have the power to carry the scheme through. They can, as they did on the last occasion, force the measure through without amendment. What amendments will be proposed I do not know. But where all should have the same interests at heart, namely, the best interests of Canada, in a matter of such far-

reaching importance, I urge the government, even at this late date, to consider whether it would not be well for them to assert a little independence of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, and say to them: ' We are not entirely dependent upon you ; we represent a great people ; you represent a great company ; we will stand by the people, you can stand for the rights of your company ; and before we will submit to the exactions which you now demand, we will nationalize this scheme ; having to build the eastern end, the difficult end, and you only undertaking to, construct a small section on the prairie and ip the mountains, we will expend a few dollars more, and will build the whole line and own and control it for the advantage of the people.'

This is the first opportunity I have had, Mr. Speaker, of thanking the right hon. the First Minister for the kindly and courteous words he used in referring to me the other night; and did I not feel it my duty to return him the compliment, I would not on this occasion venture to address the House. In my absence the right hon. gentleman referred to me in terms rather of sorrow than of anger. He said : ' My hon. friend from West Toronto, who, I regret to see, is not in his place-' I am quite free to admit, Sir, that I am not here as often as I should be, but 1 think I can claim, with some degree of justice, that I am here oftener and longer than any minister of the Crown, except the right hoii. gentleman, and surely if there ever was an occasion on -which it was the duty cf ministers to be present, it is when this Bill is being discussed. As I have said, referring to me rather in sorrow than in anger, the right hon. gentleman said :
My hon. friend from West Toronto, who, I regret to see, is not in his place, thought that he would improve the matter by having the report-
That is the report of the meeting of the Grand Trunk shareholders to consider this agreement.

printed and circulated in the House, but I am sure that the hon. member for West Toronto himself would be the first to acknowledge that in this he was wrong.
I do not acknowledge anything of, the kind.
The hon. member for West Toronto is one of these monied men and owned men of whom Sir Walter Scott speaks in a famous passage.
I would like to ask the First Minister if he would give me a reference to the famous passage. I am fairly familiar with Sir Walter Scott's works, and, while I do not pretend to be an authority, I failed to find Sir Walter Scott's passage.
Which Walter Scott ">

I thought I would draw the right hon. gentleman. He spoke of a famous passage by Sir Walter Scott, and the famous passage to which he referred is one that has only just been published. It is to be found in Sir Walter Scott's letters, which were published in the 'Century Magazine,' in 1903 for the first time, and has not yet been published in book form. The reference is not famous, it was dug out no doubt by the Prime Minister in his delight in reading Sir Walter Scott's letters, which are delightful to read, but if I may be permitted to remark, the passage has not yet become famous, because it has not been before the world more than one year, few people have ever seen it, and the right hon. gentleman no doubt stumbled upon it by chance.
With reference to the charge which he makes against me that, as a director of a public company, I will be ashamed of having brought out the stenographic report of the meeting of the Grand Trunk Railway, of course, we do not expect business knowledge from the right hon. gentleman. I suppose he would he the last man in this House to claim business experience and knowledge. He is respected for other ability and for his work in other branches, but certainly not for his business ability. Let me say that the meetings of the Grand Trunk Railway shareholders are absolutely public. At such meetings there are, as a rule, probably from ten to twenty shorthand writers sent by the leading financial papers in London. That is the case at any meeting of any important corporation. The newspapers send their shorthand writers, and there are certain stenographers who make it their business to report in full such meetings, and their reports are of great advantage and convenience. So far from being private, any newspaper in England is entitled to publish a report of the Grand Trunk general meetings in full, if they think it will interest their readers; and if you will take the trouble to look over the files of English newspapers. you will find that in every one of them there is a more or less full report of every such meeting, according as it may interest the community in which the news-

paper circulates. There was only one paper in England, so far as I know, which published practically a full report of the Grand Trunk meeting, hut had it been known that the public interest in that meeting was so great as it is in Canada, every financial newspaper would have published every word said. The right hon. gentleman states that I, as a director in public companies, ought to know that it is practically a breach ot faith to publish such reports, and that, as a director of the Canadian Pacific Railway, I would consider it a breach of faith to publish a report in full of any meeting of that comjjany. Sir, at the meetings of the Canadian Pacific Railway at Montreal, the reporters of the ' Star,' * Herald,' 1 Gazette,' and every newspaper in the city are present taking down everything that is said. Any one can go to any one of those meetings and make a full report, and, so far from such report being an improper thing, it is the ordinary part of the business life of every corporation. The Prime Minister has evidently gone back some thirty or forty years, to that period when the Hudson Bay Company and the old chartered companies considered that they were privileged bodies, and refused to admit reporters or have any report of their proceedings given to the public, except what the directors themselves chose to issue. What was the result ? Every leading newspaper in London bought, in the name of one of its reporters, a share in the company that tried to keep itself a close corporation, and a shareholder, even of one share, is entitled to go to a meeting and report whatever may he said. There is no breach of business or any other etiquette in obtaining a full report of a meeting of any public company in Canada, Great Britain or the United States. So far from my deserving censure, I am entitled to the gratitude of the House for having produced this verbatim report, so that the country may know in what light the Grand Trunk shareholders had presented to them the bargain which they compelled this government to accept. Now, Sir, the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) states that the meaning which Sir Walter Scott attached to the words of the quotation is not the meaning which I and every man in the House attached to the words as quoted.
I consider that in quoting these words the Prime Minister insulted me as I could be insulted in no other way. He insinuated, Sir, that I was a bought man, an owned man. By whom ? By the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. Sir, all my life I have been playing off my own bat.
And you made a good score too.
And I defy any man in this House or elsewhere, to say that I have ever subserved my personal feelings or personal principles to any company,, any individual or any transaction in this world.

speechtext: I can only give the explanation of Sir Walter Scotl* that it meant a landed proprietor.

In that case the explanation would not apply to me, because there is no such thing in this country as a landed proprietor, there is no meaning in words that will call a man a landed proprietor in this country and make that a sneer, or that would cause any gentleman to think that in using it he was saying something that was a reflection on a man. That is what the words as quoted by the Prime Minister mean to me. I deny the insinuation absolutely. The accusation has been made against mo in this House that I am owned by <hc- Canadian Pacific Railway Company. Mr. Speaker, if there is one thing more than another of which the Canadian Pacific Railway should be proud, it is that they have among their directors men of all political creeds and leanings. They have tried to secure and they have men who are independent in thought, and not one man in the Canadian Pacific directorate has been an owned man. Do you think, Sir, that I am advancing the interests of the Canadian Pacific Railway, by taking the stand I am taking in this House, in regard to this Eili ? If the Canadian Pacific Railway, a year ago had taken such a stand as manv of the great universities of the United States have taken, I would have been asked to resign from the directorate. In many of the universities of the United States which have been subsidized by wealthy men, the professors might be called by the term that ihe right hon. Prime Minister has applied l.) me. The professors in these universities have on many occasions been dismissed, deprived of their positions, because, forsooth, they were independent enough to teach their students theories and doctrines that were not in accord with views of the monied men who owned and subsidized these universities. The Canadian Pacific Railway has in its directorate men who are on both sides of this House, let me say men who are very strongly partisan, on both sides of this House, but I have been singled out as the one man. If the Canadian Pacific Railway acted as many of these universities nave done, they would have asked me to resign my position as director of the company immediately, because, Sir, you

can see, any man here can see, that the position I have taken on this contract, and the words I have used in this House, are not in the interests of the Canadian Pacific Railway. Do you mean to say that the position I have taken is making the right bon. the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laur-ier), the hon. the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton), the hon. the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Emmerson), more favourable to the Canadian Pacific Railway, than if I had been subservient and had backed up this scheme which these gentlemen are presenting to the country ? If I had endorsed the scheme I have nb doubt the Canadian Pacific Railway would bo treated, both now and later on, in a very much more gentle way than it is at present being treated-although I am not for one moment complaining of the treatment of the Canadian Pacific Railway. Since I have been connected with the railway they have never to my knowledge, asked what they did not think to be just and what they did not think to be their rights, and if these were refused them, they never whined. I think I have now made plain my feeling as regards the terms the Prime Minister saw fit to apply to me in a quotation which he has tried to explain away. If I were to judge from what is being done in connection with this Bill, I claim that I -would be more right to apply to the Prime Minister the words ' an owned man ' than he has to apply them to me. I do not, Mr. Speaker, for one moment apply these words to him, because I know that he is not an owned man, and I know that what he is doing in connection with this Bill is what he thinks is right and I would not for a moment suggest anything to the contrary. But, look at it, Mr. Speaker, from the point of view of hon. gentlemen on this side of the House. A proposition is put before this country involving an amount of money greater than has ever been put before this parliament at one time. The Prime Minister originally makes an appeal to patriotism, to the fear that our friends to the south would abrogate the bonding privilege. A very short time elapses before that plea falls to the ground and it has not a supporter now, it is never mentioned. Ii reminds me of the old romantic song of 30 years ago.
Oh, no, we never mention her,
Her name is never heard ;
My lips are now forbid to speak
The once familiar word.
Now, Sir, the Prime Minister and the Grand Trunk Railway Company proclaim aloud that they are partners in this transaction ; this is admitted on all hands. In ordinary busiuess transactions we know that there is a partner called the dominant partner. In this case if we go back to the introduction of this Bill, we find the Prime Minister and his colleagues endorsing this
scheme and saying that it was perfect, that it was so absolutely final, that even small amendments could not be admitted for fear of the Grand Trunk Company backing out of it. Within 30 days after the House rose, after the passage of the Bill, these men who had been so lauded as men of such repute, such position aud such condition that it was heresy to suggest that their word was not as good as their bODd, that anything they had said in the committee would be carried out without any question at all, broke their agreement. ATithin thirty days these men repudiated their solemn agreement. This agreement was signed by the president, the general manager and the leading directors of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. Within thirty days these men defaulted upon their agreement.
Mr. Speaker, on the occasion on which I addressed this House a short time ago I applied to these men the word ' fakirs.' Let me say in all earnestness and to avoid any question-I think I will not be misunderstood-that I did not apply that word, or I did not mean to apply that word to these men as individuals. I applied that word to these men as corporators of the company, and to-day, in the light of events and in the face of the lecture that I have had from the right hon. Prime Minister and others- I would expect it from the others, but did not expect it from the right hon. Prime Minister-I apply to them this word ' fakirs!' The Grand Trunk president, hi his speech, acknowledges it because he simply says : We have caused a company to be incorporated to carry out this arrangement to relieve the Grand Trunk Railway Company of responsibility. Now, as to the question of the money deposit, I think it is admitted that that was not in any shape or way the reason why the Grand Trunk Railway Company did not implement their bargain because just a week, I think, after the supplementary arrangement had been made there was no difficulty at all and the $5,000,000 was deposited. The Grand Trunk Railway Company can always command $5,000,000. The Grand Trunk Railway president and directors, like shrewd, hard-headed business men as they are, the picked business men of London and, perhaps, if that is so, we may say the picked business men of the world, because they are equal to the picked business men of the world, led this government on until they were committed body and bones to a partnership. Documents were signed, sealed and delivered on both sides. The government having responsibility to the nation, having a responsibility far beyond the responsibility attached to the directors of any private company, were bound under the agreement which they entered into. The directors of the Grand

Trunk Pacific Company having no responsibility in their corporate capacity, having put up no forfeit, proceeded immediately to repudiate their conduct, why ? They had led this government into a contract which was absolutely indefensible from the business point of view. The government had defended it. They had committed their political reputation and life to the carrying out of this contract. Mr. Hays, Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson and the other directors of the Grand Trunk Railway Compapy simply sat down. They allowed the day of the deposit of the $5,000,000 to pass without saying a word. The government getting restless, as the Grand Trunk knew they would get restless, began to apply to the Grand Trunk Railway Company. What is this ? We are in a mess. The Grand Trunk Railway Company came to the government and said : we cannot carry out this agreement as it has been entered into. We must have modifications. They knew that the government were so committed that the government had practically to take the whole arrangement into their own hands and build the road or accept any terms that the Grand Trunk Railway choose to impose. They, the G.T.R. .directors, were shrewd, hard-headed business men doing their duty to their shareholders. They were making a bargain with the government and it was their duty to make the best bargain they could. They sized up the gentlemen they were dealing with. They had no hesitation in bluffing as it is done in the American game of poker which some of the great railway men of the United States, of the older generation, have said has taught them more business than all the business in the world. The directors of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, if they are not poker players-I do not say they are-certainly knew the first rules of the game. The gentleman who held the best hand got frightened and laid down. These men came to the government with modifications of this scheme and every solitary modification that was suggested has been swallowed whole by the government. Take the first contract that this government entered into and compare it with the amendments, and you will see that there is not one single word in the amendments which is to the benefit of Canada. There is not one single word or line in the amendments which is not for the benefit of the Grand Trunk Railway Company-not one. Who got the better of that deal ? .The Grand Trunk Railway Company got the better of the deal and they deserved to get the better of the deal. They were the better negotiators and as far as the Grand Trunk Railway Company are concerned, I must congratulate them upon having at the head of that company the able men who are not afraid to enter into negotiations with the business govern-Mr. OSLER.
ment of this country and are not afraid that in these negotiations they will come out second best or play second fiddle. As I said' a short time ago, no one expected business from the right hon. Prime Minister. But we did expect business from some of his lieutenants. What have we seen '! We have a spectacle that I will be bound to say has not been seen in the chamber of any body like this in the world. We have seen the right hon. Prime Minister, whom his best friends will not accuse of being a business man, getting up and introducing this measure not as a business proposition, but as the proposition of a poet attempting to carry out a high ideal. As my hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) has pointed out, perhaps, to provide feather beds for the Indians, because, when we were looking into the narrative of one of the explorers who is quoted as an authority in favour of this scheme, we find that he says that feathers are so thick in places that the Indians and wild beasts run a risk of being smothered if they come too close to a pile of them. We all expected that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), when the matter of an expenditure of $150,000,000 or $170,000,000 was before ihisriiOUSe'TiM when the conditions under which this Bill was passed last year have been changed to such a degree that the vital control which the hon. minister quoted last year as a safeguard, namely that the stock of this company should be held by the Grand Trunk Railway Company and not given to the public, this, as he said, being the foundation of the contract, would have taken part in this discussion. But the hon. Minister of Finance is out of the House while this discussion goes on. I do not like to use any word to which objection may be taken and yet I scarcely know how to find a word which will adequately describe the situation. The hon. Minister of Finance should have been in this House during the [DOT]whole of this discussion, and he should have replied to the charges which have been made. This country is committed to an expenditure of $170,000,000. Who, on that side of the House has backed it up ? -the right hon. Prime Minister in a poetical, enthusiastic, patriotic speech and the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton) who entirely ignores the whole crux of this agreement, because he absolutely ignores the whole eastern part of the road. He does not say one word in his speech as to the road from North Bay to Quebec. Now, Mr. Speaker, that certainly does require some explanation. The hon. Minister of Finance and the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Emmerson) ought surely to be able to give some intelligent explanation tb this House as to the reason for and the meaning of the alterations which have been made in this contract.

Tlie government evidently Intended, when they brought in this amended, contract to parliament, to have it go through without any discussion at all. 1 believe myself that neither the Prime Minister nor any of his colleagues had any knowledge of what the amendments to the contract meant ; they could not have had that knowledge or they would have risen in their places to try to explain the amendments. The fact is, that during this debate the ministers have either been absent from this House, or they have sat in their seats dumb as the oyster. The Minister of Finance last session, made a very strong statement, as strong as any man could make, to the effect that by forcing the Grand Trunk Railway Company to hold the common stock and to put $20,000,000 of rolling stock on the road, the Grand Trunk Railway Company would be contributing a large sum of money-which though on our side we thought was insufficient still gave some excuse to the ministers and their supporters for believing that they had a substantial guarantee that the Grand Trunk Railway would carry out their obligations- and that this would bind them to carry out their obligations. But. Sir, every vestige of responsibility which the Grand Trunk had under the contract of last year-which 1 admit was almost infinitesimal-has been wiped away and under this amended contract they have now neither monetary nor moral obligation to carry out any part of this work. I think, Mr. Speaker, that I may take credit to myself, that when 1 spoke a few days ago, I so pierced the hides of some of these gentlemen on the other side that they were forced to get up and answer me ; that they found it would not do to let that thing go without an answer. But the answer they gave, was not an answer to the arguments that,had been advanced from this side of the House as to the weakness of the contract; it was the answer that is often given when a man has a bad case ; namely mere personal abuse. For my part, I am quite willing to take my share of any further personal abuse that may come, but so long as I am in this House representing a constituency and responsible to my people for my actions, I shall maintain my independence, and despite what may be said by any gentleman on the other side I shall sav what I think on any question of policy that is put before this parliament. It is my duty to do so, and I would be absolutely unworthy to hold the position I do, if X did not take that stand.
Now, Mr. Speaker, it has been said as part of the abuse that has been heaped upon me, that as a director of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, I object to this scheme ; the inference being, because it might be an injury to the Canadian Pacific Railway. Well, Mr. Speaker, I say that this scheme, if it goes through in its entirety as the government proposes, will be of enormous advantage to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. The Canadian Pacific Railway will, out of the money that is expended by the government, reap at least from $5,000,000 to $10,000,000 of the country's money ; which I consider is thrown away under this scheme ; but that money will come to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company- If this road is built, the Canadian Pacific Railway will not suffer in any shape or way. I have not been through the Northwest dozens and dozens of times for the last twenty-five years, without knowing that the Northwest is able to maintain not one railway or two railways, but ten railways, and probably in time twenty railways. Go, Mr. Speaker, from Minneapolis through the country traversed by the Northern Pacific, the Great Northern, the Minneapolis, St. Paul and Sault Ste. Marie roads, and I do not believe that you can travel five miles on any of these railways, without finding an opposition road crossing you or alongside of you ; and all these roads are making money and are profitable. The building of the Grand Trunk Railway in the Canadian Northwest will be of great advantage to this country ; of great advantage to the Grand Trunk Railway, and above all it will be of advantage to the Canadian Pacific Railway. Even from a selfish point of view,
I would vote for the Grand Trunk Railway getting in there every time. 1 have always advocated the entrance of the Grand Trunk Railway into the Northwest ; I do so now ; and although from my place here I have denounced the principle of bonusiug railways, at the samel time if the Grand Trunk Railway Company, or any railway company, proposes to build say from North Bay through that inhospitable and in the meantime barren region, and thence to the prairie, I would advocate a very liberal bonus towards that part of the road. When I denounced the bonusing of railways. I thought that I would have the support of the Liberals in this House. Before 1896, when I had the honour of being elected to this House, one plank in the Liberal platform was that the time had come when the bonusing of railways should cease. That is one of the planks of the Liberal platform that I approved of and adopted. It is one of the planks of the Liberal platform that I now approve of. Speaking in Torouto, long before I was a member of this House or had any idea of offering myself as a candidate, I announced that as one of the planks in my platform, and I still believe in it. even though the Liberals have discarded it with many others of the planks in their platform. Last year or the year before, I quoted in this House from the reports of the railways in the American west, to show that for twenty years no railway bonuses had been granted,' and that state after state made it the first of the amendments to their constitution that there should be no bonusing of

railways. I approved of that, but at the same time I repeat, that I would be in favour of bonusing the Grand Trunk Railway or any other railway to build from North Bay through that inhospitable region until it reaches the prairie country. I assert that there is no need to-day to give a bonus to any road running through the prairies of the Northwest. South of the boundary line you will find thousands of miles of railway built without bonuses, and you will find competition among them as to which shall first reach a section of country which promises settlement and agricultural development. We have the same conditions in our Northwest, and if this Bill should be thrown- out I believe that while the Grand Trunk Railway may regret it, yet, they would not delay for one moment to start building into that country, as they proposed to do when they first made their application tot this parliament. They will build that line I say, and they will receive from this parliament a proper, a reasonable, perhaps a generous aid for the part of their line which goes through that country and which in the meantime will not give them any return. They will do that, and they will do it just as rapidly as they would with this government giving them the enormous bonuses which it is proposed to grant.
When the Bill gets into committee I will discuss its various clauses in detail, but I assert here now, that there is not one clause in this Grand Trunk Pacific agreement which will even morally force the Grand Trunk Railway Company to send one pound of freight over Canadian lines east of the Georgian Bay. You cannot point out to me, Mr. Speaker, one single line in that agreement that will compel the Grand Trunk Railway Company to divert one bushel of grain or one pound of freight, from their lines to Portland. If I could see that in this agreement, there was provision that even at an extra cost the Grand Trunk should build up our owni eastern ports ; that they should force for a time-artificially we will say-the trade to Halifax and St. John in winter, and to Quebec and Montreal in summer it would go a long way towards making me believe that we could afford to sacrifice a lot and pay a lot to attain that object.
But, Mr. Speaker, there is not one line in all that agreement that makes the Grand Trunk Railway Company divert one pound of their freight from their great terminals in Portland. I make that charge ; it has not been refuted, aud it cannot be refuted. We on this side of the House have, I think, brought forward quietly and earnestly, very sound reasons against the contract as the government submit it to us. We believe the Grand Trunk Railway Company have the better of that agreement to such an extent that the government are in their power. The government, not knowing what they are doing, are driven into

a condition of affairs that will be disastrous to this country. Instead of trying to meet tlis condition, the government intend to force this scheme through by a policy of silence. Mr. Speaker, that surely is not dignified. The man who sits down quietly, with the strength of his majority behind him, and refuses to answer the arguments of his opponents, but says, we will beat you because we have more men, will do it, but he has not the respect of his followers, and he has not the respect of his opponents.

Mr. Speaker, it was not my intention at the commencement of this debate this session, to have offered a word of comment as respects the agreement between the government of Canada and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, as to its merits if it has any, or its demerits, for the reason that I had spoken at some length, on the subject last session, and had given no less than fifteen reasons for opposing the contract. But considering the changed condition of the agreement between the government and the company, and the concessions that have been accorded the company to the detriment of Canada, I feel I would not be doing justice to the honest electorate of the county whom I /have the honour to represent, were I not to express my views here aud tiow, on a project such as this, to my mind so suicidal to the best interests .of Canada as a whole, and to Nova Scotia, the province whence I come, more particularly Nova Scotia, which is entitled to some benefit at least, by the construction of this proposed road, but will she get it if the government intend cnly carrying the road as far as Moncton, 180 miles short of Halifax? Certainly not. Jr will not be an ocean to ocean road, and Halifax will be handicapped by being deprived of the traffic and as a result left in the cold. Halifax with its magnificent harbour, well lighted, easy of approach, well fortified, geographically offering the nearest approach to the old world, with its terminal facilities, its advantages as a coaling station, is the most important point and station on the western Atlantic.
I may ask, why should Halifax be then overlooked and, Nova Scotia's rights be ignored ?
I may be told that Nova Scotia still has the Intercolonial Railway for all her purposes, which may be true so far as it goes; but what earthly benefit would it be to Nova Scotia if it is to be handicapped, paralleled and paralyzed by the Grand Trunk Pacific ? The chief traffic it had hitherto been receiving, will be diverted by means of the arteries or branches of the Grand Trunk Company to its well equipped terminal points, Portland, in particular, in the United States, upon which it is said that company has spent upwards of $20,000,000 in improving facilities ; or if

000.000 are about being expended to meet anticipated trade, it would be taken to New York.
When I consider the unfortunate position Canada will be placed in by such an agreement or contract, and the baneful effect upon Canada, if carried into execution, of the building, for a foreign corporation, a railway, fully equipped, at a cost of upwards of $150,000,000, and when completed to be handed over to a company of aliens for a term of fifty years, during ten of which they will not have to pay interest, and by which time all the rolling stock, and probably the rails, will be worn out and worthless, I feel the whole transaction is sad to contemplate. But considering that the Intercolonial is to be paralleled and paralyzed by this proposed Grand Trunk Pacific, and left in the cold, and Nova Scotia as well, without one solitary benefit, I feel constrained to use words strongly emphasized to express my feeling of indignation. But kind words, we are taught, are more effective and productive of better and more satisfactory results, they being the music of the world. Consequently I will use them instead. It is said that kind words have a power which seems to be beyond natural causes, as if they were some angel's song, which had lost its way and come to earth. I feel that words like these may touch a tender chord-a key-note-in the heart of my right hon. friend the leader of the government, and his supporters opposite as respects the effect of their conduct, and if such words will strike him like an angel's voice bringing good tidings, it is to be hoped he may still change his mind, and so modify the character of the agreement with such safeguards as to make it acceptable to all, or, better still, accept the alternative proposition of extending the Intercolonial from Montreal to the grain fields of the west, which would cause the Intercolonial to be at once a good paying property, and prevent the exports of our Canadian Northwest being diverted over American railways to American seaports.
I feel that this Grand Trunk Pacific road, if built, will be a millstone about our necks, depriving us of other public works of a more important nature, as the immense interest on the capital we will have to borrow will exhaust our revenue and deprive us of other public works more greatly needed. I applied for a railway in my county-Lunenburg-to exteud from the junction of the Caledonia Railway at New Germany station, making it a prolongation of that road to Foster Settlement and New Ross ; and from New Ross to extend down the valley of the Gold river till it intersects the Halifax and Southwestern at or near Chester Basin. I have also applied for another railway from Lunenburg, the terminus of the Central Railway, to Park's Creek, on the east side of the La
Have river and places adjacent thereto, such as Riteey's Cove or Riverport, with a steam ferry to cross the river to connect with Dublin shore, important points, where an immense trade is being carried on. but which, up to the present, have been completely overlooked so far as railway accommodation is concerned. I hope for appropriations for other public works, such as the dredging of Lunenburg harbour, La Have river and Ma-hone bay, the completion of the breakwater at Petite RiviSre, repairs of the breakwater at the narrows of Martinis river, a bell buoy to be placed at or near Eastern Point reef, a public building for customs, post office, &c., at Bridgewater, now becoming a railway centre and an important place, and last, but not least, a breakwater at Mill Cove, St. Margaret's Bay, for protection of boats and other property of the fishermen of that place ; all which can be brought about in one year without any difficulty, for the county is entitled to these works.
But I may be told the Grand Trunk Pacific is our first consideration. Why not adopt the alternative proposition of the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden), that is to extend, as I have stated, the Intercolonial west from Montreal by acquiring the Canada Atlantic Railway 342 miles to Depot Harbour, on the east shore of Georgian Bay, and utilize the water stretches of said bay, Sault Ste. Marie canal and Lake Superior to Fort William or Port Arthur, and by the Canadian Pacific Railway to Winnipeg ; acquire or construct boats such as are now in use doing excellent work, and profitable, with capacity to carry 275, 000 bushels of wheat, equal to 275 carloads at a time, which would make transportation to the east complete in the summer season or when navigation is open ; appropriate the railway from Scotia Junction to Sudbury, and nationalize it; appropriate the railway from Sudbury to Port Arthur, improving the gradients and curvatures, and also nationalize it : also appropriate and nationalize the railway from Port Arthur to Winnipeg, and double track it By this method we can have a splendid system of transportation from west to east, over an all-Canadian route, to Canadian seaports, and with no diversion to American ports.
This would assure us success, and government ownership, and government regulation of tariff rates, the Intercolonial can be made a good paying property, and exceedingly beneficial to the general trade and interests of Canada. The Intercolonial will then be, in all verity, the people's road, owned and operated by them. By this means Halifax and St. Joint will became the.entrepot of trade and traffic from the vest, and the chief depots for all imports from the east across the Atlantic, making each city to grow and prosper, and giving employment to thousands of

hands, now struggling for a living. Farmers, by this means will find an improved market for their products, having the ad ditional mouths to supply and by which they can have improved prices, as the im-pi oved amount of shipping visiting these ports and wanting supplies will improve the demand. Farmers, mechanics, artisans and fishermen, all will be benefited, particularly the fishermen, as we by this means will have our own Intercolonial Railway direct from Halifax to the west, by which we can ship our fish in cold storage to the west and obtain our supply of flour from the east.	There will thus be no
empty cars running to the west from the east, for by the increased imports, together with our fish transportation to the west, we can have a continuous trade either way, and counteract the trade to and from Portland, Boston and New York channels hitherto supplying our Canadian west to our great discomfort and injury.
I am the more greatly impressed with the desirability of extending the Intercolonial from Montreal to Winnipeg, for by it, as compared with the government scheme, we save 461 miles, the distance from Moncton, N.B., to Winnipeg being 1,875 miles, whilst from Montreal to Winnipeg it is .only 1414, making a saving in cost to the country in construction of about $20,000,000 in the eastern section alone. As to the western section, that is west of Winnipeg. I say extend it, but certainly not to Fort Simpson, as it is only a gunshot from the Alaskan boundary, which means considerable and more than I at present desire to express.
The original agreement between the government and the Grand Trunk Pacific, introduced last session, were to my mind very objectionable, and one on which I expressed my views in a speech to the House ; but the concession accorded to the company since, giving time for the completion of the road till December 1, 1911, without a clause requiring work of construction to commence simultaneously at both ends, till all is completed, and without a restiie-tive clause requiring Canadian traffic to be routed to Canadian seaports over this line, and Canadian labour to be employed instead of alien, on construction when obtainable, is certainly not in the interest of Canada. What is to prevent this company-the Grand Trunk with all its facilities for shipment at Portland, costing it for such improvements upwards of $20,000 j00, and with all its railway connections with Portland-what is there to prevent it diverting every portion of its traffic, on reaching Winnipeg, via Pembina branch to Emerson, or St. Vincent. and thence to Duluth. St. Paul. Minneapolis. Chicago, or other cities in the United States ? Or. when reaching North Bay, diverting the traffic over its system of railways to Buffalo and thence to the seaports Mr. KAULBACH.
of Portland and Boston, or by the Erie canal upon which has been expended some $100,000,000, to the port of New York ? Is there anything in the way to prerent this diversion of traffic ? Not any. Then I ask is it fair for us as Canadians to spend a mint of money in this project to build up American cities, seaports and towns to the sacrifice of Canada ? I for one protest against it.
It was said by some of the members of the government that the cost to Canada for this project would only be $13,000,000, and some of the supporters on the other side went so far as to state to this House that it would not cost to the people of Canada one cent, whilst the president of the Grand Trunk, Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson, to his shareholders made the statement, that the liability of the company was only $15,000,000. Now I will not ask you, the members of this House, and the honest electorate of the country which is correct, but I will place the facts and figures before you and allow you to judge for yourselves. The length of this railway is supposed to be in the neighbourhood of 3,400 miles. Under this agreement the government is to build 1,900 miles-I am putting it in round figures-and guarantees three-fourths of the cost of the remainder, 1.500 miles, the Grand Trunk being liable for only one-fourth. This problem is a simple one which' any one can solve. The hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden) very modestly placed the cost of this road to the people of Canada at from $150,000,000 to $175,000,000 and a reasonable mind will view it as correct.
I approve of government ownership of railways, to control rates, and avoid combines, and in this case I feel I am voicing not only our honoured and respected leader (Mr. Borden) but the voice and sentiment of the people of Canada, who are free from party bias and willing to decide in the best interests of Canada. I say this is a view which all should accept as being feasible and patriotic, and have the Intercolonial- Canada's highway-built for and by the people of Canada, extended from Montreal into the grain fields of the west, and owned and operated as Canada's national highway, used by and in the interest of the people of Canada for the transmission of passengers and freight between the rich grain fields of the west, and the Canadian seapnrts in the cast, over Canadian railways.
The Intercolonial Railway has cost the people of Canada $70,000,000, and when extended into Montreal, the Grand Trunk Railway Company, from whom the government purchased a portion of the road between Devis and Montreal, agreed that the Intercolonial was to have a portion of the traffic routed to the Grand Trunk Railway in Montreal.
If they failed to keep faith with the government and people of Canada in the instance referred to, have we any better reason to believe they will keep faith with

Canada, as regards the contract, in routing ft eight over Canadian territory to Canadian seaports ? I say they will simply do as they please, and so will suit lEeir best interest, which will be to carry all to their own seaport-Portland.	it certainly is a humiliating position for Canadians to be placed in, and I certainly must request that the government drop all negotiations with the Grand Trunk and Grand Trunk Pacific, and extend the Intercolonial to the grain fields of the west, and thereby retain the interest and future welfare of Canada in our own hands. I say we should stand pledged to the prolongation of our own national highway-the Intercolonial, and not allow ourselves to ha taxed for building a railway, and then hand it over to a foreign company. We should emulate and in every possible way encourage transportation within our own domains, which we cannot accomplisn in any better manner than by extending our own national highway-the Intercolonial-not only by sending it to the gateway of the Dominion, Winnipeg, but beyond it, and right into the golden grain fields or garden, where we may gather the fruit, and transfer it direct to our own eastern seaports for transportation across the Atlantic to our parent home, England. Better still that we may gather the wheat into our granaries at H ali-fax and other Canadian seaports for manufacture into flour, to keep the labour in our own country, and transmit the finished articles across the Atlantic to the markets of the east. We could there see Canada bloom and blossom as a rose. Proud and de lighted should we be, occupying a country such as this Canada of ours, stretching from ocean to ocean, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, abounding in natural resources, the prospective home for millions of people.
Our climate is such as to produce and stimulate the strongest type of ripe young manhood and womanhood, physically, mentally, intellectually and morally. Our resources invite the highest inventive skill, and the very best and most earnest effort to develop them. Canada has attained a prominent place among the nations of the earth, morally and socially, in science, in arts, in literature, in commerce, in fisheries, in farming, in manufacturing, in minerals and many other matters pertaining to the interest of Canada. Her sons are the bravest of the brave, a proof of which, their bravery and their skill in the arts and tactics of war, was clearly manifest in the late war in South Africa but a short time ago, where they as volunteers offered their services, and as valiant soldiers, stood shoulder to shoulder, side by side, with the veteran soldiers of old England, and fought and bled and won on the gory fields of battles, not only fought, but died on the blood-stained soil of that country. But this is not all. We find Canadians in every portion of the world to the fore in all the struggles of life, filling prominent positions of trust, and generally prominent in every good work. Our young men, as Canadians, have attained a prominence in the solution of scientific and mechanical problems, and are distinguished for their quick recognition of that which tends to facilitate the progress of our country-Canada, and the empire as well, and the world's advancement.
With materials such as this, we on this side of the House earnestly request that the right hon. the leader will withdraw this agreement, and encourage thereby the growth of Canada by a system of transportation having plainly Canada for Canadians.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not intend at this stage of the evening to take up such an important Bill in the committee stage, and therefore I move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.
Before the committee rises I would like to ask the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) as to the mortgages to which I referred last night ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am sorry to say that I cannot give any answer to my hon. friend to-night; I shall endeavour to do so to-morrow.

My hon. friend will see, if he looks up the ' Hansard,' a distinct promise by the then Minister of Railways and Canals that the documents would be laid on the table of the House within ten days after the beginning of the session.
Progress reported.
On motion of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the House adjourned at 11.10 o'clock p.m.
